subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS

speakeroldname: Hon. Douglas Abbott (Minister of Finance) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 334, to provide for the superannuation of persons employed in the public service of Canada.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, in moving the
second reading of this bill I intend to limit my remarks to the major changes which are proposed in our system of providing contributory superannuation benefits for employees in the public service of Canada. I shall not try to cover the details of this admittedly complex piece of legislation because, as soon as second reading has been given, I propose to move that the bill be referred to the banking and commerce committee for detailed study.
In preparing this bill I have had the benefit of the valued advice of an advisory committee composed of representatives of our employee organizations and senior administrative officials, and I should like to place on record my sincere appreciation of the responsible and constructive assistance which this committee has given me. I am glad to be able to inform the house that all the proposed changes of substance have the support of this committee and that all the important points it recommended have been incorporated in the bill with one exception.
The one exception is a request that the pension benefits should be calculated on the retiring employee's average salary for his best consecutive eight years instead of his best consecutive ten years, which we are now proposing. The government has not been able to accept the cost of adding this further improvement in the pension provisions, because we believe that the other proposed major and minor modifications in the plan will place the superannuation account in a very close balance from the actuarial standpoint.
In this connection hon. members will recall that, just over a year ago, I tabled a report on the actuarial examination of the superannuation account prepared by the chief actuary of the Department of Insurance. This report revealed that the account was inadequate to meet its full estimated liability
[Mr. BalcomJ

and, even after making special credits of $75 million in each of the fiscal years 1950-51 and 1951-52 and a further one of $25 million in 1952-53, there is still an estimated actuarial shortfall of $189 million as of March 31, 1953. Steps have been taken, as hon. members know, to see that no further deficits develop and the new bill contains a requirement that an actuarial report be laid before parliament at least once in every five years. This will provide a means of determining whether the procedure adopted since that report was prepared is, in fact, adequate.
I think that I should make it quite clear at this stage that our basic objective has been to devise a plan that can be supported on the basis of equal contributions by the employer and employee to which the government would add interest. In addition, of course, special contributions, such as those which I have just mentioned, will have to be made from time to time to reduce the deficiency which already exists or to make good any new deficiency created by a general salary increase which cannot be foreseen in establishing the contribution and benefit pattern.
Taken as a whole this bill provides for a contributory system of pensions for public servants and their dependents that is in line with the best prevailing practices of government and of private industry as developed in this or in other comparable countries. I believe the proposed plan is fair to our employees and is also fair to the people and the taxpayers of Canada who, in an ultimate sense, are the employers of all those in the public service of our country.
Under these circumstances, the government cannot recommend acceptance of all the many requests that have been made for improvements in the benefits which would add materially to the cost of this pension plan at the expense of the Canadian taxpayer. If, however, several years of experience under the new plan show that there is room for some further improvements, the matter can be reviewed at that time. And, of course, if there were a general willingness to pay higher rates of contribution the benefits under the plan could be still further improved.
I turn now to a summary of the principal changes proposed in this bill. Perhaps the most important change of principle is the proposal that, in future, as I indicated the other evening, the benefits under the act will be a matter of right rather than a matter of grace, as has been the rule heretofore. Up until now, all payments under the act have been grants by the governor in council in recognition of good and faithful service. In future, payments will be matters 68108-250^
16, 1953
Public Service Superannuation Act of right with ultimate determination, if necessary, by normal judicial process. Concurrently with this change of principle we have endeavoured, as far as is practicable, to spell out all the rules and their application in the law. In as complicated and as human a matter as pension rights it is impossible to cover every conceivable situation by a clause in the act and there must therefore be some provision for the making of regulations by the governor in council; but hon. members will find, if they compare the present act with the bill now before us, that much more has been spelled out in the bill and much less has been left to regulationmaking powers of the governor in council in very general terms.
These two factors-the establishment of a legal right to benefits and the effort to put more into the bill and less into the regulations-are responsible for the somewhat greater length and apparent complexity of this bill as compared with the existing acts.
The principle I have just stated is perhaps the most important change in the legal aspects of this bill, but the change which will have the greatest impact on the whole body of the public service is the proposal to withdraw the present distinctions under the act between so-called permanent and so-called temporary employees.
If this bill becomes law, that distinction will disappear and, once any contributor has five years of pensionable service to his credit, he will become eligible to receive annuity benefits in accordance with the circumstances of his retirement. While a new employee would normally be appointed on a temporary basis in the first instance, this bill provides a waiting period of not more than one year of substantially continuous employment before such a person would become a contributor to the superannuation account. If he were appointed on an indefinite basis before the year was over, he would become a contributor from the time of that appointment.
The word "temporary" will still be used in future but it will be applied, and more appropriately, to the types of employees who were formerly -described as "casual". The new class of temporary, like a casual employee in the past, will neither contribute to nor, of course, receive benefits under the new scheme.
Consequently, unless provision is made for his retirement benefits under some other act, every full-time employee in the public service, married or single, male or female, with an annual rate of salary of $900 or more, who is not a sessional employee and

Public Service Superannuation Act has not been locally engaged outside Canada, will commence to build up his superannuation credits after no more than a year of substantially continuous employment. Prevailing rate and seasonal employees will, as in the past, become contributors to the superannuation account when they are designated for that purpose by the governor in council or when, in the case of the former, their status is changed from prevailing rate to classified. Perhaps I should point out here that, as the name implies, the Public Service Superannuation Act has a considerably broader coverage than just the employees who are subject to the Civil Service Act. This was the case under the Civil Service Superannuation Act as well so there is no change in policy in this respect.
Before going any farther I should make it clear that, while it may be some months before the administrative machinery can be adjusted to handle the great influx of the present temporary employees as contributors, any contributor to the superannuation account who retires after December 31, 1952, or the dependents of any contributor who dies after that date, will be able to enjoy any improvement in the benefits which the new act would bring. There is no need therefore for any of these persons to worry about a slight delay in bringing this act into effect. Any additional payments to which they may be entitled will then become payable retroactively. On the other hand, no change is proposed in the allowances where the retirement or death occurred prior to lanuary 1, 1953.
The general pattern of benefits under the rew act will give all contributors rights to annuity benefits after five years of pensionable service. If a contributor ceases to be employed during those first five years, the only benefit available will be a return of contributions.
If retirement takes place after five or more years of pensionable service and the contributor is over the age of sixty, an immediate annuity only will be available. If a person leaves the service before sixty because of disability or otherwise, he will have the option of some form of lump sum payment or an annuity commencing immediately, if disabled, or at the age of sixty under other circumstances. If the treasury board agrees, the deferred annuity may be paid as early as the age of fifty but reduced on an actuarially equivalent basis.
In the event of dismissal due to misconduct the treasury board will be empowered to look into the circumstances and may give entitlement to the whole or any part of

any benefit to which the person would otherwise have been entitled, subject to a minimum benefit of the return of contributions. Under the existing act the most that a dismissed person can get is the return of his own contributions which in some cases can prove to be a very severe financial penalty in relation to the offence which brought about his dismissal.
In the case of the death of a contributor before his own retirement, the widow or children will receive an immediate annuity, if he has had more than five years of service, or a return of his contributions if he had less than five years of service. Where death takes places after retirement and no lump sum benefit has been paid to the contributor, then the widow and children will receive an immediate annuity. If there is no widow or child the contributions, less any benefit already received, are payable to the estate of the deceased.
Under the Civil Service Superannuation Act, the normal annuity of a retired contributor was based upon his average salary in his last ten years of service. As I indicated earlier, under the new bill it will be based upon his average salary over his best ten consecutive years. This will be of assistance to those who, for one reason or another, may be in less well paid positions during the last years of employment.
The allowance payable to a widow and children of a deceased contributor will continue to give the widow one-half of the husband's annuity in the normal case and one-tenth for each child; but, under the present act, no matter how many children there are, the combined widow's and children's benefits are limited to 75 per cent of the husband's allowance. This bill provides for an increase in this limit from 75 per cent to 90 per cent of the husband's annuity in the normal case. This increase will be of most assistance through the insurance protection provided for the man who may die in his younger years leaving a widow and three or four young children. Similarly, the upper limit of orphans' allowances has been raised from 50 per cent to 80 per cent of the deceased father's annuity. Moreover, the $600 annual limit on each orphan's allowance has been removed as well as the $300 limit in the case of each child where the mother is still living.
At this stage I should mention the one type of benefit which is being dropped in the proposed act. Up to now an immediate allowance payable for life has been available on the abolition of office of a contributor. The existence of this form of benefit has been one of the main reasons for excluding


It is taken into account in establishing salary rates and other conditions of employment. It is, I think, wholly fitting that part of the remuneration of persons in the public service should take this form, because the security that a pension plan provides helps to ensure that independence and stability which is so important in the public service. To many of those in it, the public service cannot offer financial rewards on the scale that they *could secure in commercial, industrial or professional life; rather it offers that interest and satisfaction which arise from the nature of the work and the purposes to which it is directed. If we are to expect such employees to remain in and to enjoy their work in the public service we must, I think, provide them with reasonable security for their old age or disability so that they can, to a reasonable degree, discount the urge to seek more immediate financial gains.
As I said the other evening, Mr. Speaker, after the motion for second reading has been adopted I propose to move that this bill be referred to the standing committee on banking and commerce for detailed consideration.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of ihe Opposition):
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think there will be general agreement by all the members of the house with the statements made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) in closing his remarks when he said that it is essential that we give to the civil servants that feeling of security and certainty of employment which in itself contributes greatly to the efficiency of their work by the state of mind that this feeling in itself produces.
I feel sure also that there will be general agreement with the step that is being taken to extend to those who have been working for the people of Canada, under the employment of the government which represents them, those provisions for superannuation which have been denied to so many employees because of their designation as temporary employees. It is true that the term "temporary employee" will disappear under the provisions of this act so far as superannuation is concerned; but it is my understanding that this term still remains as a designation of those employees who are under that category so far as other aspects of their employment and occupation are concerned. I have heard no suggestion to the contrary.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext: What we have referred to as casual employees; yes.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext:
Yes. This indicates a need for going still further than this bill goes. I think this is an appropriate time to mention this fact because the approach that is made to the bill itself, when it is in committee,

will of necessity be governed in some measure by the over-all situation to which this act applies.
There are certain detailed problems which have been referred to already in earlier discussion when the motion preceding the introduction of this bill was before us and these undoubtedly can be dealt with in still further detail when the bill is before the committee, as it has been stated it will be. There are, however, one or two points that I should like to mention.
The unfortunate situation in which those in some special categories of employment still find themselves has not been dealt with by the minister in his statement today. I think that one of the gratifying features of the earlier discussion on the motion was the fact that the comments which were made were divorced from any special point of view because of a member sitting in one part of this house or in another. That is as it should be. The civil servants, whatever their designation may be, are servants of the people of Canada. They are servants who continue to serve the people of Canada whatever government may be in power or whatever the party may be from which that government is drawn.
I am convinced that there is general agreement in regard to the principles which should apply to the employment of civil servants and to the desire to create in the minds of civil servants that sense of security which they should feel in work which is of the utmost importance but at the same time does not receive the remuneration which would be given for the same type of work in private occupation.
I must say that some of the views put forward in regard to those who were employed in the Department of Veterans Affairs were of concern to every one of us. Through special circumstances relating to the history of the department, those who had been employed for some time in that department now find themselves at a disadvantage which was pointed out when this subject was under discussion. There is no indication that this situation is to be covered by anything now before us. Nevertheless, I would hope that when this measure is before the committee there will be an opportunity to make recommendations in regard to amendments to apply to that relatively small, but still substantial, number of employees of the Department of Veterans Affairs whose position has been prejudiced by events entirely beyond their control. I trust that this will be dealt with, and dealt with along the lines suggested in the discussion which has already taken place.
Public Service Superannuation Act
Consideration should also be given to the fact that the calculating of superannuation for appointees is on the basis of the last ten years of service. I do think there are reasons why this in itself does produce inequalities which have been pointed out, and which I am sure will be pointed out to the committee. Very strong arguments have been put forward that the basis of calculation should be the last five years. That view has been expressed by representatives of the civil servants themselves and by representatives of the veterans' organizations, and I hope it will be given due consideration when this committee is considering possible amendments to the proposed measure now before us. That and other related subjects, however, can be dealt with at that time.
The very fact that we are now expressing our general approval of a plan to bring under the provisions of the superannuation act those who have been described as temporary employees for so long emphasizes in itself the necessity for a general review of the situation, and the inclusion of all those employees affected by this act and similarly beneficial provisions under any legislation which would end any distinction of that kind.
An effort should be made to equalize, not only from the point of view of supervision, but from the point of view of status, security of employment and other provisions of that kind, all those who have worked for long years, and have long ago demonstrated by the length of their employment the fact that they were not temporary employees. To the extent that this measure brings to an end or, shall we say, reverses the tendency to increase the proportion of temporary employees in relation to permanent employees, it should be welcomed by everyone in this house as well as by those employed in that way.
In explaining the general provisions of the measure now placed before us for consideration, the Minister of Finance has spoken of the so-called permanent employees and the so-called temporary employees. That was a very apt term. The employees are only so-called temporary when they work as temporary employees for ten, twenty, thirty and forty years, as some of them have. There is however this fact which we must recognize. There has been a steady increase in the relationship of the number of temporary employees to permanent employees. In 1939 the temporary employees were a much smaller percentage of the total than they are today. In 1939 the number of temporary employees was 43 per cent of the number of permanent employees. Today the number of temporary employees is 126 per
3948	HOUSE OF
Public Service Superannuation Act cent of the number of permanent employees. In fact the figures, as of December, 1952, which would presumably represent the general situation fairly accurately today, show that there were 56,936 permanent employees and 72,200 temporary employees.
The measure now before us provides for putting temporary employees who have at least one year's service on the same basis for pension purposes as permanent employees; but so far as I am able to interpret the statement made to us, or the bill now before us, it does nothing about those special problems relating to employment which are substantially affected by the difference in designation. It has a provision with respect to veterans, but it will still remain for the committee to make sure that those provisions are effective and deal adequately with the special problems of veterans in relation to civil service employment.
Without doing more than seeking to emphasize the considerations which should be before the committee which will have wide-open discretion to review the sections and consider proposed amendments, I would point out that when We start to discuss the question whether the basis of computation should be eight years, ten years or even five years, as recommended by the representatives of the civil servants and veterans' organizations, we realize how unreal the word "temporary" is in relation to a great deal of this employment.
This measure automatically brings some
60.000	of the temporary employees within the provisions of this act because of its coverage of those who have at least one year's employment. But there still is a very large number of temporary employees who are outside the provisions of this act. The figures which are before us show that to be the case, since the figures of the department show that there were 72,200 temporary employees as of December last.
This indicates that there are still over
12.000	temporary employees not affected by this measure. It is true that, as their employment might continue and they might meet the condition of a year's employment, they would find themselves under the provisions of this measure.

speechtext: What I am emphasizing is that in dealing with this problem, which is a very real one, in a way which I am sure meets with general approval in the house, I urge that we recognize what this demonstrates. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: It removes that, completely.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext:
It removes that difficulty and
injustice so far as superannuation is concerned. This is in fact a step to render justice to those who have been designated improperly as temporary employees of the government of Canada. And when I use the word "improperly" I am not attributing any improper motive. But it is a practice that has grown up; and by the figures I have shown it has had the habit of extending itself.

I suggest that in dealing with this matter we should recognize that fact, and that we should adopt the attitude that this is the recognition of a principle which should be extended still further to the civil service of this country, and that we should end the unreality of the term "temporary" in relation to those who have had steady employment for some period of time.
I do not intend to deal with the sections one by one, because they will be discussed by the committee. Many of them carry out rather involved provisions in regard to the method of computation. There is one section however to which I should like to refer, one which I believe is very satisfactory, and that is section 28. This section provides for reciprocal agreements in respect of the transfer of employees. I believe that is a very satisfactory arrangement, and one which should be encouraged. It should be applied wherever possible in connection with the transfer of civil servants from one government to another. More and more there is an increasing field of joint activity between the dominion and the provincial governments. I am sure for that very reason it will be extremely advantageous to the public service of Canada generally if civil servants of the dominion and of the provincial governments may be transferred from one service to the other, without disrupting their continuity .of employment, or their continuity of contribution to superannuation. In fact, the more that there may be an even standard of civil service employment across Canada, the better it will be for the public service generally.
I am not suggesting for one moment that anything done by this government should encroach in any way upon the authority of provincial governments or legislatures. But the very fact that such agreements can be worked out will widen the opportunity for the exchange of civil servants in those branches of employment where it may be that a civil servant of the dominion government may perform a more useful service at some point in the administration of a provincial government or vice versa.
I support the general principle of the bill. And in discussing the points I have made I would ask not only that they be given consideration in committee, but that also we acknowledge this step as a recognition of a general principle which should apply to the whole service; and that the name "temporary" should cease to be used in respect of people who long since ceased to be temporary employees, as shown by their years of service.

We are pleased with the way the minister puts it, when he says that pensions under this legislation will now be a matter of right rather than of grace. In point of fact, there may not be a great deal of difference in the actual awarding of individual pensions. But certainly the terminology and the idea behind that approach is all to the good.
We feel that the introduction of the legislation at this time is an indication of the growth of the idea that all those who render service to their day and age are entitled to the reward of a dignified and decent retirement allowance, when their years of service are over.
I have no intention of going beyond the bounds of the legislation before us; but I do think it is permissible for me to say that we welcome the legislation, not only because of the rights that it extends to public servants, but we welcome it as a part of a growing body of legislation that provides security for all our older people. We hope that that body of legislation will continue to grow, until we have adequate security for all. We will continue our efforts in that connection.
I said the other day, and I repeat now, that while we are glad to see the so-called temporary employees being brought under the act to the tune of including some 60,000, we feel that there are groups of prevailing-rate employees who have not yet been given the benefit of this legislation, and who should be included. I realize of course that further legislation to extend the benefits of this act to other prevailing-rate employees is not necessary. All that is necessary to take in further prevailing-rate employees is for the governor in council to designate such other groups as coming under the provisions of this legislation. speechtext:
Now we all know what we are talking about and we are all talking about the same thing. We now know that the government has improved the legislation slightly in that it has changed the provision from the last ten years to the best ten years. But we also know that the government has rejected the proposal of the advisory committee that it should be the best eight years. I am sorry that the government did not find it possible to accept that recommendation. I note, for example, that in the new pension plan of the Canadian National Railways the provision there is that the pension is based on the last ten or the last 

five years of the employee's service, whichever is to the benefit and advantage of the employee. After all, the Canadian National Railways is owned by the government of Canada and there is a case where, true by option but certainly at the option of the employee, a five-year period may be taken as the standard for determining the pension. Because a five-year period is considered in that case, I am sorry that the government has stuck to the ten-year period in this case. It seems to me that the recommendation made by the advisory committee for a period in between ten and five, namely, a period of eight years, was a very responsible one, and I hope that even yet that figure will be given consideration when the bill goes before the committee.
There are still other provisions that the minister has announced today which we think are all to the good. We feel that the provisions he has announced with respect to lump sum payments and the provisions for widows and children, where changes have been made, are all to the good, and I am sure that all who are interested in this measure will welcome them. I think it was also very fitting and timely that the minister should announce today that the pertinent provisions of this measure will be retroactive to December 31, 1952. He made the particular point that any employees who have retired since the first of this year will not lose the benefits which they otherwise would have gained if they had continued in the service up until the time the act is passed, given royal assent and put into force.
As I say, that is a welcome announcement for any who have retired since the first of January but it is tough news for any who retired in November or December of last year. I see that the minister is smiling. I know he will say that it is always the role of the opposition, even when something is good, to suggest that it might have been just a little better. Therefore we are not out of character in that respect, but in suggesting and asking as I do that the retroactive date be put back to an earlier point of time I have good reason for making that request. The minister knows that when the speech from the throne was read in February of 1952 opening the session before this one, it was announced that there would be amendments to the Civil Service Superannuation Act, and we expected that the bill that we now have before us would be introduced during the 1952 session of parliament.
As that session went on and it became apparent that the bill might not be brought in, there were some civil servants who were

fearful lest the government's delay in bringing the bill before parliament might cost them the rights they would have under the legislation. Accordingly, Mr. Speaker, on June 23, 1952, I put this question to the Minister of Finance on the orders of the day, as recorded at page 3547 of Hansard, for that date:
May I direct a question to the Minister of Finance? Would it be possible for the minister, before this session ends, to make a statement as to whether or not the amendments to the Civil Service Superannuation Act, which have been put off until the next session, will include a provision making the terms of those amendments retroactive to whatever date would have been the effective date had the bill been brought in at this session, as was indicated in the speech from the throne?
The minister replied as follows:
It would not be possible to do that, Mr. Speaker.
Then the next line of Hansard contains that little word that sometimes appears in Hansard in italics, the word "later" in brackets, which means that not right at the moment but a little later in the day, in fact I believe before questions on the orders of the day were concluded, the Minister of Finance thought better of the answer he had given me and stood up and said:
Perhaps I should supplement the answer I gave the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. It is possible that some of the changed provisions of the Civil Service Superannuation Act could be made retroactive, but I think it is unlikely that all of them could be.
As a matter of fact, though neither of us said it in that exchange, I am sure that both of us were thinking of this very problem, the problem of those who would retire before the benefits of the new legislation would become effective. In view of the fact that the government announced in the speech from the throne in February, 1952, that the amendments would be made at the 1952 session, and in view of the undertaking which the minister gave the house in reply to my question on June 23, 1952, I think that the question of the retroactive date should be reconsidered. If the bill had been brought in and passed in the 1952 session I do not know what its effective date would have been, but I am sure it would not have been December 31, 1952. It probably would have been December 31, 1951. At any rate, all the employees of the government who retired between the date that the announcement was made in the speech from the throne in February, 1952, and December 31, 1952, lost out. They get none of the benefits or improvements that are made available to those still in the service or to those whose retirement did not take place until after January 1, 1953.

Mr. Speaker, we also welcome the way in which the act is being changed so as to provide for greater mobility of employment as

Public Service Superannuation Act between various agencies of the government and the civil service proper; also as between the federal civil service and provincial civil service; and also as between service with the federal government and service with the international agencies and other such bodies. As the Leader of the Opposition said a few minutes ago, this is certainly all to the good and we welcome it. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, I hope that it will not take too long until we establish this principle on an even wider basis than just as between different types of government service. One of the characteristics of our society today, as we build up these pension plans, is that in many cases workers are frozen in a type of employment for fear of losing their pension rights or for fear of taking lesser pension rights than would otherwise be the case. It seems to me that there is definitely room for increasing mobility of employment by arranging for greater transferability between all pension rights-not only between different types of government service but between service with different private employers, and between private and public service. That is an ambitious program to take care of, but one way in which it can be facilitated is for the government, through the same minister we have before us now, to provide the proper kind of income tax deductibility for those pension plans in private industry which are funded in such a way as to provide mobility, or in other words to make it possible for employees to leave one employment for another employment, and yet take with them their pension rights.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, what I am saying is that if this principle is desirable in terms of public service we feel that it is desirable generally. I feel, to the extent that society recognizes the right to dignified retirement in old age, the right to security in old age on the basis of service rendered, and makes sure that it is a reasonable amount, to that extent society is making progress.
I am also glad that the minister has announced the provision which seems to have the effect of re-opening to those who have lost it the right to elect to cover past service. speechtext:
I hope this can be gone into more fully by the committee.
There are one or two things which the minister seems to have forgotten. Well, he

has not forgotten them, but he has overlooked them and I regret to say that I feel that it has been deliberate on his part with respect to this bill. He heard the discussion the other day, when we were at the resolution stage, with respect to the employees in the old soldiers' civil re-establishment department who have not yet been given the right to transfer to part II of the Civil Service Superannuation Act. The minister will recall the discussion because just about every member who took part in the debate urged that a change be made. In response to that urging he made a rather lengthy statement which, of course, left the door open for further consideration; but it indicated that the minister did not feel that this change should be made at this time. Frankly, as I listened to his argument and tried to analyse it, it seemed to me that it was this in the main. To make this change in favour of these employees who are still in the service would be, so he said, to give them a right which many who have long since passed out of the service or passed on did not get. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, it is not a very good argument to say that because some others did not get something that was their right, those who are left behind should not have that right either. He might argue that it was not a right, but common sense does seem to suggest that those employees should have been given this right long ago. The mere fact that those who are not now in the service or those who have since died did not get it is, I suggest, no reason why it should not be extended to the few hundred who are still here and who have been discriminated against in this way. I have no doubt that if the committee will hear delegations on various points, there will be a delegation with respect to this matter. I trust that the committee will give it very earnest and sympathetic consideration.
I think we all approve of the suggestion made by the minister this morning with regard to the elimination of the obligation that public servants generally should retire at 65. Generally speaking, I think there is merit in his suggestion that pension rights, from that point on, would be frozen. I wonder, however, about the case-there will be some like it, I imagine-of a person who, at the age of 65, has not yet obtained many years of pensionable service? Will such persons be denied the right, if they are kept on in employment, to build up their years of service for pension purposes? The act places a limit of 35 years on pensionable service, and that seems to be a reasonable proposition. In other words, the top possible pension is 35/50ths of one's average salary for his best ten years or 70 per cent of that
Public Service Superannuation Act average salary. Since you already have that ceiling, why impose another ceiling on people who may have come into the public service late in life? There may be angles to that which can be gone into, but I hope it will be considered.
I have just one other observation to make, Mr. Speaker, with respect to this bill. I think after .all the fine things I have said about it the minister will not be surprised if my next comment is one of very severe condemnation. My guess is that he knows what is coming. I condemn the government very strongly for failing to include in this bill a provision for an increase in the pension of those already retired, particularly those in the lower brackets. The minister knows from repeated comments on this matter on the floor of the house, and repeated representations from those affected, how serious is the plight of those people. The figures are on Hansard. I have seen to it that they have been put on every year for a long time, but in this session they are shown at page 510 of Hansard for December 10, 1952. I shall not read them in detail, but I shall indicate that these figures show that out of 10,572 retired civil servants, 1,468 are on a pension of less than $60 a month. In fact, 312 are on a pension of less than $20 per month. The figures for widows of civil servants, who number 5,123, show that more than half, 2,766, are on a pension of less than $40 a month, and 942 are on a pension of less than $20 per month.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext: But some of those are people with very short service. Perhaps they acquired a pension somewhere else before they went into the public service.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext:
There is always an explanation from the minister, either short service or they were employed in the days when Bennett was reducing salaries, but the point is that these pensions are too small to enable people to live on them. The minister tries to tell us every time this matter comes up that you cannot indulge in retroactive legislation of this kind. However, at least two provinces, Newfoundland and Saskatchewan, have made some legislative provision for people who have retired on small pensions. The minister knows that on two or three occasions when the United Kingdom had legislation like this, they provided for an increase in the pensions of those already retired. Similarly, in the United States in 1948, an act of congress was passed which increased the pension of retired employees by 25 per cent or by $300 per year, whichever was the lesser figure.

Public Service Superannuation Act Then, in 1952 a further increase was granted by another act of congress. The result of these two pieces of legislation works out, for example, that a superannuitant who was receiving $1,000 per year was increased in 1948 to $1,250, and in 1952 to $1,565.50. This example, of course, is in a little higher bracket than is the case of the figures for Canada I gave a few minutes ago, but the principle involving a percentage increase is there, and that would be of at least some assistance to those in the lower brackets. For their sakes, however, I believe a better formula is possible. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the continued reluctance on the part of the government to deal with this matter is most reprehensible, and it is a source of bitter disappointment that when an otherwise good job-I say that without qualification despite the few points upon which I have criticized the bill-is being done, these people are left out in the cold.
On January 12 of this year, I asked one of my frequently recurring questions on this point, and it appears at page 891 of Hansard for that date, in the following form:
Has the government given consideration to the provision of a cost-of-living bonus or other increase m the pensions of federal civil servants already retired? If so, what is the result of such consideration?
The reply is as follows:

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS

I have looked back at that answer a good many times, of course, and all it says is no. What I think is most annoying to the people who are affected is that, for a few years, there seemed to be a growing willingness to consider the matter. Since that statement appeared on Hansard for January 28, 1949- it had been issued publicly a few days before -there has been no apparent reconsideration of this whole problem. This is the case despite the fact that I have before me letters from officials of organizations of retired civil servants in various parts of the country who get a certain amount of encouragement out of letters they receive from the minister, from other ministers and from members on the government side of the house, telling them that the matter will be considered.
As a matter of fact, on January 28 of this year the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) apparently wrote to Mr. J. O. Belanger, the provincial secretary of this organization in Quebec city, assuring him that his representations would be considered when the superannuation act was under review. Well, it

Mr. Speaker, I should like to take just a few moments to say what I think about the bill that is now before the house. My first words should be ones of commendation of the minister for bringing in this new bill to replace the old superannuation act and for the comprehensive changes for the good that have been incorporated into the bill.
When one is considering an act of this kind, it seems to me that it has to be considered against a certain well-defined background. In this case I think we ought to keep in mind that the background is this. I am not going to go into the matter at too great length, but, Mr. Speaker, by policies which we have laid down and slavishly followed we have actually condemned to spending the remaining portion of their lifetime in perpetual poverty a great many Canadian people who gave of their best while they are employed as civil servants. I do not believe that is the right thing. I am sure the minister would not want to do that. We simply cannot go on slavishly following policies that will condemn people to poverty.
Many of these people were not able to work after they were retired. Many of them have not been able to find any gainful employment since that time. Remember that the government is responsible in large measure, because of the policies it followed, for the decline in the purchasing value of the dollars that these poor people have been given. Since that responsibility must rest on the government, then I say that the government is obligated to do something for these people.
I am not saying in this act, but certainly in some other act they can bring in.
Let me impress upon the government this important point. They must know that this country is capable of producing sufficient goods and services to enable these old, retired civil servants, who are on a miserable pittance, to have a decent living. There is no doubt about that. What we have to do is to set our minds to the task of finding a way of getting these goods into the hands of the people who can use them to bring up their standard of living, so that we can at least hold our heads up and not have to go about hanging them in shame.
I say to the minister, we are prepared to help him find that way. I know as long as he follows the present financial policy it will be virtually impossible for him to find a way to help these retired civil servants whose purchasing power today is only half what 

it was in 1939. I say it is time we were looking for another act, and we should bring in a piece of legislation that would make it possible for us to get the goods we can produce into the hands of our own citizens who can use them. There is no sense in condemning them to a lifetime of poverty just because we have not yet had sense enough to discover and put into effect at least a decent policy.
But let me say this: I must congratulate the minister on all these fine changes that have already been mentioned-I do not intend to take up the time to go over them again in this house-which are contained in the bill. The introduction of this bill does mark a real step forward in our consideration for Canada's employees. It is certainly far beyond anything we have had in the past, and the minister certainly deserves commendation for it.

I do not think that anybody at any time in this country would criticize the minister for listening to these people and granting them some relief under this legislation. With that as a preamble I want to draw the attention of the committee to some discrepancies. I began to do so last night at the time the minister was saying that I was actually killing time, and I will try to do it as briefly as possible. In the white paper at paragraph 130 this statement appears:
Of the fourteen minesweepers now under construction, six have been launched, with the remainder to be launched during 1953.
In the statement or in the article by the chief of the naval staff there is this citation:
Coastal minesweepers, wooden, . . .14, all under construction, eight have been launched.
At page 3920 of Hansard the minister says:
All fourteen of the coastal minesweepers have been launched . . .
Now there does appear to be a very great difference to say the least in those figures. The minister's white paper claims that six have been launched; the chief of the naval staff says that eight have been launched; and the minister corrects himself and says that all fourteen have been launched. Obviously somebody is launching ships the minister did not know about until yesterday.
I would like him to comment on that.
In paragraph 129 of the white paper we have this sentence:
A total of 52 new vessels are on order, including escort vessels, minesweepers, harbour craft, inner patrol vessels, clearing diving vessels, tugs, crane lighters, a northern patrol craft and auxiliary vessels.
In other words all the types of ships that are being built for the navy are enumerated in that section, and they total 52. Now, again, somebody is fooling somebody but I do not know who it is. In paragraph 130 again, and I think I mentioned this last night, we have the statement:

In the article by the vice-admiral, there appears this statement:
Anti-submarine escort vessels, 14-(nine under construction, three of them launched; . . .

A prototype of Canada's new anti-submarine escort ships, the former destroyer H.M.C.S. Algonquin-

I want to draw to the minister's attention again an article in the Montreal Gazette which was quoted last night by the hon. member for Kootenay West, which referred to statements made by the chief of the naval staff in a press conference in Ottawa. The article is dated Ottawa, December 17, and reads in part as follows:
The admiral, who this month took over command of the E.C.N. and who two years ago wrote the "Mainguy report" on the navy's internal problems, said at a conference in the parliamentary press gallery that he, as chief of the naval staff, is "against" any R.C.N. activity or development which does not have to do with anti-submarine work or the defence of harbours.
I believe that statement, or practically all of it, was quoted last night by the hon. member for Kootenay West. I am repeating it, Mr. Chairman, because I think it is very important. It strikes us in Newfoundland very forcibly. It must be recalled that during the last war we had enemy submarine activity brought right to our doors. In my own riding of St. John's East, at Bell island, the wharf of which has been discussed with the Minister of Public Works on several occasions-I sent him a picture of the wharf at Portugal Cove the other day, and I believe he perused it with great benefit to himself-there were three ships loading ore which were sunk by submarine torpedoes. We had submarine torpedoes discharged against the harbour of St. John's, which struck the rocks on each side of the harbour. We had the Caribou, which ran between North Sydney and Port aux Basques, sunk with a great loss of life. We had a lot of enemy submarine activity. So, Mr. Chairman, I think it is only right that this particular part of the defence of Canada be given the consideration which the chief of the naval staff says it deserves. I am sure my friends from the west coast of Canada will feel the same as we from Newfoundland feel about it, that too much stress
Supply-National Defence cannot be laid upon the part the submarine will play in any war that may come in the future.
As the chief of the naval staff said in this article which was quoted last night, Russia now has as many submarines as Germany had at the zenith of the last war, and she is building them even faster than Germany did. With this very real menace, then, 1 think Canada has to face up to the fact that the only way you can fight a submarine-I am merely quoting what I have heard those very much more competent than I say-is with planes and surface craft. The most forward eastern base in Canada is in Newfoundland. We do have United States forces in strength there, and I presume they will continue to increase if war appears imminent. It is not quite fair, however, to leave the defence of Canada to the United States, no matter how willing or able she might be to undertake it.
In that connection, we have a very fine airport at Gander, Newfoundland, which has been operating, as you all know, for many years. It was of great help during the last war in the patrolling of the seas in and about Newfoundland, and assisting in convoy work. The airport at Torbay was also of very great assistance, as was the airport operated by the United States navy at Argentia. At the present time there is no land communication between those three important airports, that is between the United States base at Pepperrell, which uses Torbay airport, the United States base at Argentia, and Gander airport, except the narrow gauge railroad operated by the Canadian National. There is no road connection of any kind. I understand the western provinces are now planning to make representations to the cabinet concerning the necessity for the construction of an all-weather defence road for the west coast. In my opinion the construction of a proper broad highway for defence purposes in Newfoundland is really of even greater importance. I suggest to the minister that he take into account the urgent necessity for communication between Gander airport, Torbay airport and the United States base at Argentia. I believe the matter has been discussed-I do not know whether or not it has been discussed at high levels- and the ranking officers of both forces, off the record, have said that they are in favour of the construction of such a road. The road is of equal importance to the United States and to Canada.
I believe that, given the proper approach, such a road could be constructed on a fifty-fifty basis between the United States and Canada. At the present time the United States forces have constructed or rather

Supply-National Defence have materially widened a road to their base at Argentia known as Salmonier road. They have put a lot of money into the rebuilding of that road, and the maintenance of it. I feel that, in so far as the defence of Canada is concerned, the convoy routes of the future are the great weakness of our defence on this side of the Atlantic. We have to depend upon surface vessels to supply our allies on the other side of the world in time of war, and they would have to cross that dangerous body of water, the north Atlantic. I urge upon the minister that consideration be given to the construction of such a road.
As the minister knows, the United States navy maintains quite a large and extensive base at Argentia. There is a very narrow neck of land between the bays known as Placentia bay and Trinity bay. If it were possible that a canal could be cut across the neck of land at present known as La Manche it would enable United States vessels to go from Placentia bay into Trinity bay. If war came it would be of great assistance with respect to the time saved. At the present time you have to steam from Placentia bay all the way around past St. John's and past Conception bay to get into that area. I think it would be well worth while to investigate the digging of a canal. Then of course the peninsula of Avalon would become an island. It might be quite expensive to carry out such a project but I think it is well worth while investigating.
The last matter to which I desire to refer is this. I do not wish to delay the committee unduly but I wish to draw to the minister's attention, and to get his views on, the question of an armoury at St. John's for the reserve units. As the minister knows, term 44 of the terms of union between Newfoundland and Canada says this:
Canada will provide for the maintenance in the province of Newfoundland of appropriate reserve units of the Canadian defence forces, which will include the Newfoundland regiment.
I am quite certain that the minister will appreciate the fact that the word "maintenance" obviously means the providing of an armoury for a unit such as the Newfoundland regiment. There is no other way that we can get around that word. "Maintenance" definitely means what it says. After all, if you guarantee to provide for the maintenance of any person, it means that you must provide a house or some other building in which such person would be housed or kept. In this particular case, where Canada guarantees to provide for the maintenance of a regiment such as the Newfoundland regiment, I say it is part of the terms of union that an armoury should be provided for this

reserve unit. I hope I have not left the minister completely in a fog with regard to the matters I have discussed.

Mr. Chairman, in the statement he made in the house last Tuesday afternoon, referring to the Royal Military College of Saint-Jean, Quebec, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) made the following remarks reported at page 3808 of Hansard:
The candidates of the two languages mix and work together, and virtually all of them now speak both languages. These men will constitute an important pool of officers of great value, particularly today when the nations of the world are intermingling more freely.
Further down the minister added:
So great has been the success of Saint-Jean, and so desirable is it that this operation in military training as well as in national unity should be extended, we are going to make provision for a total strength of 400 cadets.
I wish to say immediately to the minister that I readily agree with him. The question of national unity is very near to our hearts. Government members like to raise this question as often as possible and they will surely appeal to those sentiments on every possible occasion during the critical period which might very well be the political menopause before the snow flies, this year.
I hope that in making that statement of principle the Minister of National Defence was sincere and I am ready to grant him the benefit of a reasonable doubt. However, during the few remarks I intend to make this afternoon, I will afford him the opportunity of giving us concrete and practical proof of his sincerity. I simply intend to bring to his knowledge a condition which, unfortunately, prevails very close to this house, and to request him to remedy it, as it should be, if he really wishes to contribute by deeds and not only by words, to the strengthening of the bonds of true national unity across the country.
In taking part in this debate, this afternoon,
I will stray to some extent from the line which I have conscientiously tried to follow ever since I came to this house, that is not to take part in any debate on questions which I was unfamiliar with and which had little or no relation to the interests or economy of my constituency or my province. I might add right away that I know very little about military matters and I am quite ready to confess, Mr. Chairman, that I am no authority on militarization, and much less an adept of militarism. Nevertheless, if I make so bold as to rise to take part in this debate it is;

because, to my mind, there is a principle involved, and that is the recognition of the rights of French-Canadian airmen at the Rockcliffe air station as regards the teaching of religion and of the French language to their children, and more particularly to the children at the Woodfalle school.
Let us for a moment consider the situation from the school and educational point of view at the Rockcliffe air station. Then I shall point out briefly what certain responsible and independent newspapers think about this matter.
Well, the situation at the Rockcliffe air base, from the school and educational viewpoint, is simply awful. The real concept of education in the true sense of the word seems to have been forgotten and it seems as though it is being wilfully ignored. It seems that this concept which should include, first of all, the imprescriptible rights of the parents, then of the church and thirdly the suppletory rights-and they are only suppletory-of the state, is being wilfully ignored. The recognition of these rights is being ignored at Rockcliffe, especially the first two, that is the imprescriptible rights of the church and of the parents in matters of education, which are the most important. And it is the authorities of the Department of National Defence who are responsible for this situation.
The Rockcliffe school was built with the money of all Canadian taxpayers and I find, on page N-52 of the public accounts for 1952, that the sum of $514,704.99 was spent for the construction of an 18-room school at Rockcliffe. Now, from a pedagogical standpoint, the school at Woodfalle apparently follows the program of the province of Ontario while refusing to apply that section of the Ontario law which allows the establishment of separate schools where the teaching of the French language and of the Catholic faith could and should be given.
Mr. Chairman, if we compare Rockcliffe to any other area, we find that the treatment meted out to French-Canadian Catholics is worse than the treatment they endured under the famous regulation XVII. At Rockcliffe, national defence authorities are not satisfied with restricting French; they exclude it altogether, along with the teaching of religion. Whereas the school system of the province of Ontario recognizes both the public and separate schools, the national defence authorities have adopted at Rockcliffe the public school system while refusing to recognize the separate school system.
Supply-National Defence
Such is, in brief, the situation at Rockcliffe air base, as I see it from the school and educational viewpoint.
Now, to come to the second point I want to make, let us see what the independent and right-thinking newspapers of this area think of this situation and what they have to say about it.
Here is, first of all, an article published in Le Droit of January 26, 1953, under the title "A situation worse than under Regulation XVII". I quote:
But what has the Department of National Defence done at Rockcliffe airport? It has refused to provide accommodation so that the children of Catholic and French Canadian airmen may receive an education which would be French and Catholic in character, in accordance with their rights and the dictates of their conscience. If those airmen wish to send their children to school at Rockcliffe airport, they have to send them to the local public school, where teaching is done exclusively in English.
The Department of National Defence is worse than the Whitney government.
The writer mentions again the famous regulation XVII and he adds:
True, French Canadian and Catholic airmen can send their children to bilingual separate schools outside, but that changes nothing in the situation which prevails at Rockcliffe airport. Due to a decision taken by the Department of National Defence, there is only one school at that station, the public school, which is neutral and English.
On March 20, 1953, Le Devoir had an article entitled "The Rockcliffe Affair", of which I would like to quote a paragraph:
Rockcliffe is a suburb of Ottawa. An air base has been established at that place and it so happens there are children of school age.
A certain number of those children are Catholic. The authorities have forgotten to provide the necessary facilities to enable those children to receive, at the base proper, an education in accordance with their religious beliefs.
Lastly, I would like to quote a paragraph from another article, published in Le Droit of March 17, 1953, entitled: "The Conspiracy of silence, at Rockcliffe, must come to an end". I quote:
During the past several years, the army has made it a point to give greater importance to the French language and to count more and more on the cooperation of the French-speaking element. We do not know what the situation is with regard to the navy, but we seldom hear complaints. However, in the air force, it is rumoured that in several places, young French Canadian members of that military body do not always receive fair treatment. There are more than false rumours in that connection and specific cases have been stated. They don't appear to be general in scope. The responsibility for these unfortunate happenings has, so far, fallen upon officers of inferior rank and only in a few training centres. We cannot infer from these incidents that an anti-French Canadian policy prevails in the Canadian air force.

However, at Rockcliffe, there is no school where Catholics of both languages may send their children. This is a condition absolutely contrary to a true national spirit, contrary also to the provincial statute, which regulates matters of education in military camps. It is very urgent that this question be straightened out: no question of economy nor any other minor consideration should intervene here. This is a matter of right and Catholics of both languages should take every means to defend that right.
Before bringing my remarks to a close, I wish to call the attention of this house to the steps I have been taking since last January 28 in order to obtain the following documents:
For a copy of all correspondence exchanged between the federal government, or any department thereof, and any person or persons, in connection with the teaching of religion and French to the French-speaking pupils of Woodfalle school, Royal Canadian Air Force station, Rockcliffe, Ontario.
An order for return was passed by this house on January 28 but I am still awaiting the production of these documents. Three times I rose to ask the Secretary of State (Mr. Bradley) about this matter. In the first two instances he answered that he would do everything he could to expedite this return. Last Monday the Minister of National Defence rose to tell me that his department was quite willing to provide me with these papers, but that permission ' was being requested from a provincial government, which, at my request, he admitted was the government of Ontario.
Will the Minister of National Defence allow me to tell him that his last excuse is very clumsy. Why should he insist on obtaining the agreement of the province concerned before producing these documents, since my question did not refer to any correspondence exchanged between his department and the province of Ontario or any other province.
I merely asked for the correspondence exchanged between the federal government or one of its departments and any other person or association concerned. Moreover,
I must say that the documents I asked for are not numerous and that a secretary could have prepared them in two hours at the most. However, I am still waiting.
Mr. Chairman, as Le Droit so rightly puts it:
The conspiracy of silence, at Rockcliffe, must come to an end.
We are not behind the iron curtain, but I note that there are certain curtains which should be ripped open. And I think that the curtain-be it made of velvet or some other cloth-which closes the opening of the tent under which the Minister of National Defence 

takes cover, and which will not admit our search into his department, should be the first to be thus ripped open.
Mr. Chairman, in closing 1 urge the Minister of National Defence to prove his sincerity by deeds and not by words; to remedy the unfortunate and iniquitous situation which exists in the school and educational field at Rockcliffe air base, only a few miles from our parliament. I would also ask him to produce at long last the papers which I asked for more than ten weeks ago.
Mr. Chairman, I ask the hon. members of the House of Commons to excuse a young member, a newcomer, a backbencher who admitted being quite ignorant about military matters, for having been so bold as to stand up in order to stress the glaring injustice inflicted upon his fellow citizens at Rockcliffe. If I have done so, it is because I believed, and still believe, that it is my duty to defend the principle involved. Like the chief of the apostles, I could say, in the very words of Peter to the sanhedrin:
For we cannot but speak after what we have seen and heard.

Mr. Chairman, I have been following the defence debate in the house rather carefully, as hon. members well know. It appears to me that the official opposition has given the debate a new twist. Something new has been added. In previous debates on the same subject their slogan was: Waste, extravagance and inefficiency. We on this side of the house said: "Point to the evidence. Where is the proof?" The opposition have now added a new twist to the slogan by adding: We have inadequate home defence. Thus a new plank is being added to their platform, and1 the new slogan will go something like this: The official opposition will be saying to the Canadian people: "You are spending five billions of dollars. You have inadequate home defence, because of waste, extravagance and inefficiency." That will be repeated on many platforms throughout the country. I think the place to say it is here, and I say it now- that that is the greatest hoax ever played on the Canadian people. It is a nice trick if you can do it; but you will not.
Let me for a moment examine this question of waste, extravagance and inefficiency. Let us take the normal case we all understand, of the possession of a refrigerator. A refrigerator in the home of a civilian worker is a normal requirement. When this government provides the same refrigerator, but at

a lower cost, in the serviceman's home, it immediately becomes waste.
Let us take the case of the landlord who plants a tree, sods his grounds, and keeps the place in good repair. We consider him a good Canadian citizen and also a good landlord. But when the government provides the same service to the serviceman, at once it becomes landscaping, and therefore an extravagance.
Then, wading pools, which are normally provided for children of civilians in parks throughout the country, when provided for servicemen's children under similar circumstances become frills and fancies.
The small carpet, when provided normally in a civilian's home, becomes, when it is provided for a serviceman, a rug. And when it is described on the hustings, it seems that the servicemen are walking knee deep in them, or perhaps, only ankle deep.
Let us take the case of the bed lamp found normally in most homes. When a bed lamp is provided for a serviceman it becomes a boudoir lamp, with all sorts of connotations.

Then, when we ask where those luxurious camps are located1, when we ask about those houses with the gilded door knobs, the usual answer is: Wainwright. We are told there is a swimming pool at Wainwright. Well, Wainwright is in the middle of the prairies, and if there is any place in the country that needs a swimming pool, it is Wainwright. Isolated as it is, if we provide a bowling alley and a gymnasium, and a chapel, I do not think we are doing too much for our servicemen.
The official opposition has the advantage of hindsight which, of course, is a great advantage. They can say what should have been done, and act like the Monday-morning quarterback. However, I think that before they pursue that course any further-and I am of the opinion that they believe they have made about as much political capital as they can out of waste, extravagance and inefficiency, because they are not playing that record with as much vigour as they did on other occasions-they should listen well to what the Canadian public are thinking. I suggest that the editorial which I am about to read, and which appeared in the Canadian Military Journal, an independent defence forces review, reflects the views of the Canadian public. This is what appeared in the Easter issue under the heading "Unjust Criticism":
For many months past there have been many disparaging comments by Canadian newspapers and
Supply-National Defence news commentators about the pampering of the personnel of our armed forces.
Such critics have appeared to resent the fact that our National Defence Department has seen fit to spend money on furnishing our soldiers with bedside tables and lamps, with carpets, mirrors, bureaus and other such whatnots.
In our opinion such resentment and carping criticism are entirely unjustified. It should be remembered that the great majority of the well paid working men in Canada have all of these things in their homes. So, why should the men who work in our armed forces be deprived of them? These same harsh critics of reasonable comforts for sailors, soldiers and airmen, when off duty, are the first to belabour the Department of National Defence if it fails to secure the number of recruits necessary for our armed forces. The very fact that we are apparently now getting an adequate supply of recruits is, we think, in some measure due to the publicity that has been given in the press to the fact that, by joining the armed forces, a man will not be deprived of the amenities that he has become accustomed to as a civilian.
No! The days of old when it could be truthfully said that, "a soldier's life was one of extreme hardship, unremitting toil and damned poor pay" are over-and we are glad of it! But, even in peacetime, there are still lengthy periods of each year, the training season, when a soldier still has to undergo much more toil and hardship than a civilian,-but, if he is reasonably well paid, as he is now, he has no complaints.
We think that it is high time for the critics, above mentioned, to cease their misguided attempts to deprive the men of our armed forces from enjoying the same home comforts as the civilian workers. They may not have much longer to enjoy them. If they happily do, it will be because their strength, added to the strength of our allies, is forcing on Soviet Russia the necessity of continuing to postpone world war III.	[DOT]

Then, of course, I also mentioned the increase which had taken place throughout the services, the navy, the army, the air force and so on. The minister had something to say in answer to the Leader of the Opposition and me in regard to the lack of equipment in the reserve forces. The minister did not really deal with this lack of equipment, but mentioned particularly carriers and jeeps. He said that if the units were losing carriers, they had been taken away for repair, I think it was, and the jeeps had been taken away but were being replaced by some kind of general service truck. That may be, but I know that I have been getting these complaints that units have lost their jeeps, and I certainly do not hear that they have been replaced by anything comparable. The minister did not go into some of the more important complaints, such as the lack of directors in the artillery and other technical equipment of that sort; the lack of guns themselves, and so on. He did say something about breech rings. These guns were being sent back to have the breech rings changed as a safety measure, although the guns have been in use for years and years. However, it may be

necessary to do that, but I certainly do not think you needed to take away all the guns from the unit at one time in order to do that. The removal of the guns could have been staggered so that a unit could have continued training. There was no necessity to interrupt or destroy unit training in order to change the breech rings. The lack of directors and other technical equipment was not dealt with.
The minister said something which really discouraged me. He said the units were trying to get down to the amount of equipment that they need so that they could carry on more efficiently. I would ask him if any of the units were trying to get rid of their directors; have they been trying to get rid of their jeeps or their guns? It is complete nonsense to say anything of that sort. The units have been complaining very strongly about the way in which equipment has been taken away from them. The minister says it was taken away to please them. It is really not a very sensible statement.
So far as equipment generally in the reserve forces is concerned, I do not think there is any question at all but that there was no need for any of the units to suffer in their training or in their morale as a result of the removal of material from them. It could have been removed in shifts if it were being taken away to be repaired, and then returned. If it was being taken away to be sent overseas, it should have been left with the unit until the new equipment had arrived to be put into their hands. In this way the unit would not have been left without anything.
In that connection, one of the particular complaints concerns the anti-tank regiment, with which I happen to be personally familiar. Some two or three years ago the anti-tank regiments lost their guns. In some places those anti-tank guns were replaced by 25-pounders, and the units were told to train on them. Since that time none of these units have known what their situation is. They do not know whether or not they are anti-tank regiments. The generally expressed opinion is that the anti-tank branch of the artillery is being eliminated, and that the job is being taken over by the armoured corps. It may be a good thing to do that. Certainly a reserve force unit which is designated in a certain way, and left to train in a certain way, should not be left up in the air that way, with their regular normal equipment taken away and replaced by different sorts of things, and more or less in a position where they do not know where they are at. I think perhaps the time has come for the minister, during this debate, to make a definite statement as to what is to be the fate of the anti-tank artillery, whether they are to continue with that or whether

they are going to be converted into something else; and if so what it is and when this will take place, so that these units will have something definite to strive toward in the future.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I should like to join with other hon. members who have taken part in the discussion of the first item in the estimates of the Department of National Defence, and in doing so I shall deal with a matter vitally connected with the community in which I live, and one which has been close to my heart through many years. I refer to the plants of A. V. Roe Canada Limited at Malton, Ontario, where aircraft and the Orenda engine are produced. This subject has been debated in the house on former occasions. Perhaps the background of the Malton plant should be described, because up to this time that phase has not been mentioned by the minister or others.

speechtext: Order. Perhaps it has not been mentioned by the minister because it might be discussed more properly under the estimates of the Department of Defence Production.
