speechtext:
I think there is, Mr. Chairman. It will be realized as I go along that the Malton plant plays a very important part in these estimates, and that a considerable amount of the money to be voted will go to the production of aircraft at that plant.
In the late thirties Malton airport site was chosen. Since 1936 the airport located there has developed until it has become the greatest in Canada. Alongside it grew up, first of all, the plant of what was known as the National Steel Car Company. Then Victory Aircraft was established. And now, after the close of the second world war, we have located there A. V. Roe Canada [Mr. Applewhaite.l

Limited. All three of these organizations manufactured aircraft.
At the present time A. V. Roe Canada Limited employs in its two plants-the original one and the new Orenda engine plant-over 13,000 men and women. The company is one of the largest employers of labour in the whole metropolitan area of Toronto and, I suppose, one of the largest employers anywhere in Canada.
It has been a matter of considerable pride to me, as the member of that constituency and living close to the plant-because I suppose I live closer to it than any other member, and for that reason have been able to see it more often-that we have at that point in Canada such a magnificent industry, which not only has made a good record up to the present time under almost impossible circumstances, but which also is giving to Malton the distinction of being the centre of the Canadian aviation industry, both in peace and in war.
I am one who has always championed and supported the industry at Malton. It has not always been popular to take that position because, as most hon. members know, there have been criticisms. These have not been confined to parliament or to any political party, but have been made because people have not always understood the gigantic difficulties and obstacles those three companies, including A. V. Roe, have faced from time to time; difficulties which are being overcome today by A. V. Roe Canada Limited in connection with the production of the Orenda engine and the CF-100 with its various marks which are now being designed and will be produced later on.
I have always felt that if there be criticism it should not be directed against the management or the employees of the plant, but rather against the departments of government. It can be said, in simple language, that in an aircraft manufacturing policy there are, speaking roughly, three alternatives that could be followed. First of all, the plant could build large numbers of obsolete aircraft on a high-speed production line, and show to the public a tremendous record of numbers produced. But when they were produced it would not necessarily follow that such aircraft would have any major value in our defence program.
A second alternative would be to do no designing and no original research work at the plant, but rather to obtain licences from someone, or from some other country, that has originated designs. Then those models could be put on the production line and,

again, a great showing could be made as to the number of aircraft coming off the assembly line.
Those alternatives, however, have not been followed at Malton. I am one who believes that the alternative chosen has been the proper one. In the plant, since the close of the last war, with a large amount of government assistance the A. V. Roe plant has succeeded in setting up a research, designing and developing team which has now reached the point where there are few better such teams to be found anywhere in the world. They have produced in their plant what we believe, and I think the government believes, is the best jet airplane engine, and the best aircraft of its type in the form of the various marks of the CF-100.
Having chosen that alternative, one cannot expect the same amount of production, or the same quantity off the assembly line, as if the other alternatives had been followed. After all, the very last word in production, design and manufacture of both engines and aircraft is coming off the assembly line in the Malton plant.
That brings up another aspect which is of very great importance to that area. We feel that the designing, research and development team ought to be kept intact so that when the current international tension and impasse have subsided there will be a great peacetime centre of the civilian aviation industry there which will of course be of great importance to Canada in the days that lie ahead. That is the reason I think the proper course has been followed, and I hope the government will not change its policy in that respect but will pursue it despite the fact that there has been considerable criticism from time to time of the number of planes that have come off the assembly line at Malton.
There is one other matter to which I should like to refer, and that is the untold difficulties and almost impossible obstacles that have faced the management and employees of the plant during the last few years. It is hard enough to produce aircraft and engines in a pioneering atmosphere such as we have had at Malton, but one of the greatest problems arises from the fact that just when the design is ready to go on the assembly line for manufacture the Royal Canadian Air Force or some department at Ottawa asks for some minor, or sometimes major, change in the design which again stops production for weeks and sometimes months. It is a pretty discouraging situation to find that from time to time such changes, which seem to occur more often perhaps than is necessary, are holding up production on the Malton assembly line.

I think the minister should consider having a somewhat closer liaison between those who are experts at the plant in these matters and the Royal Canadian Air Force and his own department, so that consultations may be held and agreement reached to bring about fewer of these minor and sometimes major changes in the structure of the plane itself, thus allowing the plant to proceed more rapidly with its manufacture. If that were done I am quite sure there is a possibility of the planes and engines coming off the assembly line much more quickly than they have in the past.
I make that constructive suggestion to the minister because I am anxious, just as he is, to see to it that the position of A. V. Roe Canada Limited is brought to as high a position in Canadian estimation as it is possible to achieve. It does seem to me that perhaps the Malton plant is now, to use the language of the street, over the hump, and I am satisfied that the plant has a management team and group of employees who are capable of doing an extremely efficient and effective job for Canada and our forces generally. I think it can be said that those in the present set-up at Malton know where they are going and how to get there. I think that sizes up the situation the department will now find in the plant. I believe the plant deserves an opportunity to show what it can do, and I should like to see it get that chance with as few obstacles as possible placed in its way by those who are directing or giving orders with respect to the requirements of the air force.
If this is done I am convinced that the plant will turn out in satisfactory numbers the kinds of planes and engines that are expected of it by the people of Canada. I can remember quite well when the little village of Malton was not a very important point on the old Grand Trunk line and later on the Canadian National system running west from Toronto. It has grown since 1937 until it is now a major centre in industrial Canada. I believe that the plants there now, together with the airport, will be responsible in the days that lie ahead for Malton not merely being a village or a town but one of the great industrial cities of Canada and the central point of our aviation industry in Canada, and perhaps even in a broader sphere.
I wanted to make that point clear because the question of Malton's success is a matter affecting a great many people in my constituency. I am not sure how many people in the county of Peel work there, but there must be somewhere between 3,000 and 5,000. Generally speaking working conditions are good, and I think the employees are, in the main, satisfied with conditions. I am anxious, however, that there shall be full co-operation

Supply-National Defence between management, employees, the research, designing and development team and the department so they may all go forward together in a co-operative enterprise and demonstrate that today there is no better or more effective plant for manufacturing engines and aeroplanes anywhere among the NATO nations than the plant at Malton.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to go over the same course twice, as was suggested by the hon. member for Skeena, but unfortunately the Minister of National Defence in making his reply yesterday omitted to answer two of the questions that I raised and rather brushed me aside on the third one. Therefore I must return to the attack.
I was endeavouring to find out in the first part of my remarks yesterday, which dealt very briefly with casualties, the exact figure of our casualties to date. I pointed out to the minister that in response to a question I had raised in the house in the first week of February I received a reply to the effect that our casualties as of the 31st of January numbered 1,335. Today's paper contains casualty list No. 172, which gives the total as 1,304. In his remarks yesterday the minister mentioned a figure of 1,300. Why can we not have the exact number? I asked for a correct statement in so far as casualties are concerned.
The second point I dealt with was the problem of ammunition, and I have been dealing with this ever since the last week of November. Not for the first time did the minister suggest that to discuss this problem would have a bad effect on morale. Yesterday he said, as appears at page 3927 of Hansard:
I suggest that this is a matter on which hon. members should exercise the usual caution which should be applied to matters affecting the morale and welfare of the troops.
A similar remark was made by the minister in December. I would suggest to the Minister of National Defence that questioning in the House of Commons concerning the ammunition situation on the field of battle is all to the good, that the morale of the troops who are actually engaged in battle and the morale of the troops about to go to the field of conflict will be heightened by their knowledge that the House of Commons is intensely interested in their equipment and supplies, and particularly with regard to the amount of ammunition on hand. Their morale will be heightened because the House of Commons is eager to see that no pains are spared to ensure that a full supply of ammunition is available. That will raise their morale, and not lower it. I think the worst thing for men serving overseas in any type of war is to feel that they are forgotten and that their interests are being
[Mr. Graydon.l

neglected. There is nothing in what we have said here in the House of Commons that would tend to do other than raise the morale of the troops overseas. It shows that we are not forgetting them and that we know what is going on.
My regret is that the minister yesterday and the day before did not give us a full account of the situation in Korea. For example, I asked him if we were employing Korean soldiers in conjunction with our troops. I had a question on the order paper some time ago asking for that information and the answer I received was no. One week later there was a press report to the effect that Korean troops were going to be used within our Korean battalions. Well, we are left in the air again.
Yesterday I asked the minister whether we were making use of the protective clothing that has been devised, clothing which has some armoured component in it. The minister did not comment on it, but I think it is an important matter and that we should know about it. The thing which disturbs me so much about the matter of defence is that a veil of secrecy is drawn over things that need not be secret, and we are depending so much on press reports. We are not getting information here in the House of Commons. I think a great deal of credit is due the people who furnish us with so much of this information, but I think it would be better if we received that information directly in the House of Commons.
With respect to the ammunition problem that I have raised, the minister considered that my argument was dismissed by certain quotations which he made from a debate in the House of Commons at Westminster and from a newspaper report of what President Eisenhower had said. The minister, at page 3927 of Hansard, quotes from a reply by the British prime minister to Mr. Shinwell as follows:
I am informed that the ammunition supply in Korea has always been sufficient to meet the operational requirements of the United Nations forces, and shortages of ammunition have not restricted the planning of operations.
I would draw the attention of the house to the fact that Mr. Winston Churchill has admitted in his statement that there have been shortages of ammunition. Why we cannot get the same admission in the House of Commons here, I do not know; but on March 9, when I asked a question of the Associate Minister of National Defence with regard to ammunition supply the answer was given, as it appears on page 3726 of Hansard, in these words:
-there is no shortage of ammunition in respect of actual operations.

Then the Minister of National Defence quoted from a press report concerning what President Eisenhower had said, and I shall just repeat four lines which appear on page 3927 of Hansard:
President Eisenhower said yesterday there is sufficient ammunition in Korea for present scale operations and then described the supply situation as perfectly sound under current circumstances.
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that these statements do not stand up under analysis. Mr. Winston Churchill's statement admits that there has been a shortage of ammunition. He says that shortages of ammunition have not restricted the planning of operations. Well, of course not; they never do. You can always plan if you have one round or a thousand rounds. If you have a thousand rounds you may attack, but if you have one round you plan to sit tight or perhaps retreat. You can plan under any circumstances, having regard to the amount of ammunition you have available. General Van Fleet pointed out exactly the same thing in his testimony. Of course, you keep your planning going; but during the last several months it has not been possible to plan for anything more in Korea than to sit tight and take it, and 1 think that is what our troops have been doing. They have been sitting tight and have been shelled unmercifully by the Chinese. I think we have not had sufficient ammunition for counter-battery work to knock out enemy guns.
We have President Eisenhower's statement that there is sufficient ammunition in Korea for present scale operations. Of course there is sufficient for present scale operations. If you are not doing anything, if you are not going to fire any ammunition, if you are not going to make an advance, perhaps you do not need any.
I will recall to the minister's attention the situation that prevailed on the western front in 1915 of which he is aware, either from firsthand knowledge or from reading about it. There was a shortage of ammunition in those days and operations were planned continually; but the operations were cut short, as I pointed out in an early speech in this house, on instructions from the high command that the operations should come to a conclusion. The reason? No ammunition. That is why I have been raising the question of ammunition in the house, hoping to get a reply along somewhat different lines than I have received.
We have the admission from the minister that whereas in December we were on the American supply line, now, for certain types of materials, we are on the British supply line. That is useful information and perhaps
Supply-National Defence we are better off on the British and Canadian supply lines for ammunition for the 25-pounder gun, a type which is not American and which is used in the commonwealth division. I understand that our supply of ammunition for those guns has been reasonably adequate.
Will the Minister of National Defence, who should have the information, say whether we are on the American supply line for other things which General Van Fleet said were in short supply, such as mortar shells and grenades? I do not know, and who does know? Unless the Minister of National Defence can supply the information we are left in the dark. The suspicion is that there is a shortage of mortar shells and grenades.
The average Canadian who understands the productive capacity of this country fails to see why we cannot come forward and offer to assist. Are we supplying ammunition from Canadian sources, and, if so, why can we not be told? I have seen press reports since this disturbance in the United States with regard to ammunition shortage indicating that Canadian sources were being tapped to supply ammunition. That is all to the good, but why cannot we be so informed?
As the situation stands at the moment I think my queries with regard to ammunition have been rather brushed aside and we are left in the uncertain position of not knowing whether our troops in the field have a full and complete supply of ammunition, not only to sit in the trenches and be shelled until casualties occur every day, but ammunition sufficient to knock out enemy guns. Also I asked a question about our ammunition supply in Europe, which press reports say is below the required amount. No answer was given to that.
My third point yesterday had to do with the Royal Canadian Armoured Corps, and I emphasized the fact that it was being neglected under the present circumstances. To my regret the minister failed to heed that particular section of my speech yesterday, for I thought he would make some comment on it. He did say one or two things with regard to armour. We have been suggesting from this side of the house that more armour should be made available. We have suggested an armoured brigade for Europe. My statement on that is in Hansard on more than one occasion.
I have noticed, Mr. Chairman, that you can have a first-class argument if those who are participating do not talk about the same thing. It might even develop into a row. For purposes of this debate, however, I think we should discuss the same thing, and I suggest to the minister we should discuss the
3978	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence same thing. The point I was discussing was an armoured brigade, and according to page 3921 of Hansard for April 15, 1953, he transforms that into an armoured brigade group.
Here are his words:
We have the type of unit we were asked to provide and which fits into the scheme of things on the other side.
I would be inclined to ask for more explanation with regard to that particular sentence, but I shall pass on to the next.
It enables us to train and operate independently as a unit, but an independent armoured brigade group working in isolation from a division or a group, as I have said before, is a military monstrosity. We have never heard of such an organization, and it could not operate.
Then farther down he says:
-in order to create the unit that has been suggested, as we understand it, we would require larger forces than the present ones.
Let us talk about the same thing. Let us talk about an armoured brigade, and let us not talk about an armoured brigade group. I have never mentioned an armoured brigade group. I am talking about an armoured brigade. I say that if we maintained an armoured brigade in Europe and an armoured brigade at home, we could then train the Royal Canadian Armoured Corps as it should be trained and deserves to be trained. We would maintain a proper balance in the army.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext: Perhaps we can find out if we are talking about the same thing. May I ask the hon. member if that would mean an armoured brigade in addition to the present infantry brigade or in substitution for it?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext: I suggested yesterday it would be in substitution for it. I suggested an armoured brigade in Europe and one at home, and an infantry brigade in Korea and one at home. You would then have replacements. There would be an infantry brigade in Korea and an infantry brigade at home.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext: And an armoured brigade in Europe?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext:
And an armoured brigade in Europe, as well as an armoured brigade at home. The situation now is that we have an infantry brigade in Korea, one in Europe, and what have we here? There is one at home. There is one on its way to Korea and one on its way back; that is about the way it works out. There is a parachute brigade, and then the one in Europe.
If we are talking about the same thing, an armoured brigade would use about 510 fewer men than an infantry brigade. You would have increased fire power and effectiveness through mobility with an armoured brigade as compared with what you have in


an infantry brigade. I am speaking now of the situation in Europe. With about 510 fewer men, you would have 144 heavy guns in the tanks which would exceed the artillery component now attached to the brigade over there.
I wish to draw that to the attention of the minister, because I felt we were certainly discussing things which were not normally comparable. He was able to brush aside this suggestion of an armoured brigade for Europe because he said we were talking about something which was a military monstrosity. I think, Mr. Chairman, that it would be possible to devise formations that are not necessarily in accordance with war establishments as to the last man or the last gun that is required. During the course of the war that was done frequently. All sorts of formations were organized which might be called, by some people, military monstrosities. They turned out to be very effective. I suppose some people would suggest that Wingate's forces which were used in Burma were a military monstrosity, or that the desert patrol which operated in North Africa was a military monstrosity, or the special service battalion, and so on. I have not been discussing anything of that nature. I have been discussing simply the well-known armoured brigade.
In the last war we had the first and second armoured brigades. The British had several of them. The eighth British armoured brigade was very well known, and its strength was effectively used in conjunction with infantry formations. Why could that not be done now? The infantry formations supplied by other nations in Europe could be supported" by the Canadian armoured brigade. That is what I am suggesting to the minister. I think this neglect of armour in the Canadian army is a very serious matter indeed, and could be corrected if steps were taken along the lines I have proposed.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, two or three points remain on which hon. members have asked for information and on which I shall be glad to do my best to give them that information.
With regard to the question asked by the hon. member for Gloucester relative to the school at Rockcliffe, we were in the position where we had a considerable number of married quarters, and no school accommodation was provided by the local school authorities. In accordance with the practice we have followed right through the Department of National Defence wherever that condition exists, we established a school at Rockcliffe. It was established in accordance with the laws of Ontario. We follow that practice in each case where we have to establish a school.

The school was set up, the teachers were appointed, the curriculum was established and it was operated in accordance with provincial practice.
Then the school was later taken over by the city of Ottawa. The area surrounding it became part of the area of the city of Ottawa. It has continued in operation in accordance with the provincial law. If anyone has a suggestion to make that it should be divided or dealt with in some other way, I suggest that is a matter to be dealt with in accordance with the law of Ontario, and in accordance with arrangements made between the city of Ottawa, the province of Ontario and the Department of National Defence. We are complying with the provincial law.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext: Does that mean that the Department of National Defence has nothing to do with the school at Rockcliffe?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext:
Oh, yes; we operate the school in the same way that we operate every other school we have. We have about 40 schools for the children of serving personnel. We have them in nine out of the ten provinces in Canada. In each case we operate the school in accordance with the law of the province. We make arrangements with the board of education, under which a school board or similar body is set up to operate the school. In Ontario, we have schools at Barriefield, Borden, Rockcliffe and a number of other places as well. All are operated in accordance with arrangements made with the province.
The most usual arrangement is that we contribute the capital cost of the school, just as the local school corporation would ordinarily contribute the capital cost, and then the province contributes whatever proportion it would contribute to a school of that size and in that locality. Usually it is 50 per cent of the cost of maintenance. The province approves the selection of teachers, who must meet provincial requirements.
Academic standards, textbooks, inspection and the like are all according to provincial standards. The school operates in the same way as does an ordinary school operating under the provincial system, the only difference being that instead of having a school corporation there is the Department of National Defence which usually appoints the commanding officer at the station and the required number of others to constitute the school board or committee. In the case of Ottawa, however, because of the fact that the school is in the area which has been taken over by the city of Ottawa, we are now working under arrangement with the city of Ottawa.
Supply-National Defence
With regard to casualties, I overlooked the fact that the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre had queried the number. The number he gave was apparently picked out of the Canadian Press report which was arrived at by totalling the figures of casualty lists as they are issued without making subsequent adjustments. The number, as at April 15, 1953, is 1,322 battle casualties and 77 deaths from ordinary causes, making a total of 1,399.
The hon. member for Nanaimo called my attention to an error I certainly made, but which I might explain by saying that when we refer to a destroyer escort vessel or ship we think of a new modern type, none of which has yet been commissioned. The article in question referred to destroyer escort ships and in that more general category were included the modified destroyers which he had in mind. The hon. member for St. John's East also made some remarks with regard to the statistics relative to ships, and in order to make this matter perfectly clear perhaps I had better go over the facts again.
On April 14, 1953, at page 3810 of Hansard, I was reported as saying that we have in active operations 56 ships. That is not correct. If Hansard correctly reported me, then I was speaking without notes at the time and I did not make the full statement that appeared in the white paper as I intended to do, because in the white paper I stated that we expected to have 56 naval vessels in commission during 1953-54 and, in addition, a number of other auxiliary vessels.
With regard to naval vessels under construction, we have actually placed orders for 53 naval vessels, including auxiliary vessels, and are preparing to let contracts for 18 others, making a total of 71. Of these, 26 naval vessels and 10 auxiliary vessels are as of this date actually under construction.
This all relates to orders placed in Canadian shipyards. In addition there is H.M.C.S. Bonaventure which is being pressed on to completion at the shipyards in Belfast on the other side.
With regard to the observations of the hon. member for St. John's East with regard to discrepancies, between the article In Canadian Shipping by the chief of the naval staff and other statements, I would like to say again that these deal with different time periods. At page 25, paragraph 129 the white paper shows a total of 52 new vessels on order.
The article by the chief of the naval staff, at page 82 of the March issue of Canadian Shipping, shows the total number of ships in the approved program as 72. This latter
3980	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence figure includes 18 ships the construction of which had been approved but for which contracts had not been let at the time the white paper was drafted. It so happens that the white paper and this article were prepared at a time when considerable changes were occurring in the figures. This article also includes five Gate vessels which, as is noted in the table on page 82 of the article, were completed but not under construction.
The white paper, in paragraph 130, states that six of the fourteen minesweepers hav6 been launched and the article refers to eight having been launched. Two were launched during the period between the dates used in the white paper and in the article.
In my statement at page 3920 of Hansard for April 15 I said that all these minesweepers had been launched. By this I meant that I was informed that all had reached or passed a state when launching would have been practicable; but as hon. members know, in certain shipyards-for example, in Saint John, New Brunswick-construction is continued on the ways while in other shipyards the hull is ordinarily placed in the water while the ship is being completed.
Then the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre referred to the question of body armour. I must say that I had not known of his inquiry at the time. We are using the lightweight body armour that has been developed in the United States. It is on issue to units of the commonwealth brigade in the proportion we agree on. We also have developed in Canada and have under further investigation a material which is comparable in stopping power to that at present in use. It shows promise of improvement in some other characteristics.
With regard to mutual aid, on checking over my notes I find that I did not answer a question asked by the hon. member for Nanaimo as to the shortfall. There it appears that, on the best figures so far available for the fiscal year 1952-53, there will be a shortfall of approximately $90 million. This is made up as follows; direct production, $9 million; air crew training, $7 million; equipment from the second world war, $32 million; a change in the method of charging for F-86's on mutual aid account, $9 million, although in the latter we are 40 per cent over our target on deliveries; equipment, $6 million. That makes a total of approximately $93 million. On other accounts we have delivered $2 million more than is estimated, arriving at a net shortfall of about $90 million.
With regard to the question of ammunition, raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, the objection I take to his remarks-and I hope he will not mind my


repeating it because it seems to me to be a perfectly reasonable objection or comment when one is responsible for raising troops-is in the use of such phrases, if I have noted the words correctly, as "shelled unmercifully because of lack of counter-battery activity." I think that was the phrase the hon. member used.
We have no evidence or report, and there is nothing in the record anywhere to indicate any basis whatever in fact for that assertion or suggestion. It is on that account-and I hope the hon. member will excuse me-that I say that on such matters one must speak with a great sense of responsibility. I described the situation with regard to ammunition before proceeding to the last meeting of the North Atlantic council, as we understood it, and I supplemented that description yesterday.
We are in this position in the Korean war. We are part of the commonwealth division and as such, with respect to most items, we are on the commonwealth supply line which largely comes from British sources. Sometimes we put articles of equipment into that supply line, but do not ship them direct to the Canadian brigade. In this way we sent at one stage 200,000 25-pounder shells to the commonwealth supply line. They were used by all the forces of the commonwealth, all of which are equipped with 25-pounders. But for other types of equipment Canada, unlike the other commonwealth countries, is relying on the United States supply line and that applies to other guns, our Sherman tanks and some other weapons. It would be totally uneconomic and impossible, I think, for us to set up a separate supply line of our own. And we work in close co-operation with the other countries.
The situation regarding ammunition was as described in the statements of Mr. Churchill and President Eisenhower, but I will go on, if the hon. member wishes, and read from the testimony of General Van Fleet when speaking before the Senate armed services committee on April 1:
Senator Kefauver: I believe you testified in previous testimony that all of the troops in Korea, from whatever nation they came-except perhaps the English and Canadian troops-were supplied with American ammunition. Is that correct?
General Van Fleet: No, sir. The British supply their own ammunition.
Senator Kefauver: I say all except the British are supplied with ammunition from this country.
General Van Fleet: Yes.
Senator Kefauver: Do the Canadians supply their own ammunition, or do we supply them?
General Van Fleet: We supplied them. They were equipped with our -105 Howitzer initially; but as I understand that today, they are using the British -25 calibre.

We were never equipped with the -105.
I continue:
Senator Kefauver: So we are probably supplying some of the Canadian units, and the English are supplying some of the Canadian units.
General Van Fleet: No, sir. I think it is all British today. The British division has organic artillery entirely of British make.
Senator Kefauver: How did your ammunition supply for our troops and for those that we were supplying compare with the reserves and the use by the British division that is in Korea?
General Van Fleet: I have never heard of a shortage of British ammunition.
Senator Kefauver: Do you know whether they had a larger proportionate supply than we did?
General Van Fleet: Their commanders stated they had a good supply.
Senator Kefauver: You do not know the details about that?
General Van Fleet: Yes, sir, I know the quantity they mentioned to me, which was greater than our quantity. I think that quantity is confidential. I will tell it to you in executive session.
I suggest that these statements taken together indicate that for the purpose of operations we have had the ammunition we needed. Now it is perfectly clear to anyone who has had any experience in battle that nobody has ever had, or ever will have, all the	ammunition	they	want.	General
Bradley made an amusing reference to that in his own evidence in answer to a Republican congressman, Dewey Short, General Bradley said:
No artillery man ever had enough ammunition to shoot, any more than any preacher ever had a large enough congregation.
That is well known to all of us. Therefore in times of relative inactivity like the present the troops are rationed in the use of ammunition-they are often rationed during battles, as everyone knows-they are not rationed and they are not short when they need the ammunition for purposes of fighting, on occasions of great danger; and that is the position as I understand it today. But I think the fact is that despite all this talk about the shortage of ammunition, the United Nations forces have been firing ammunition at a rate which is ten times that of the forces who oppose them, and very much greater than all but the most extreme rates of either the second or the first world wars.
The hon. gentleman suggested that it would be better if he got this kind of information in the house rather than from press sources and press releases. Well, if the house spent its time getting this kind of information or that on aeroplanes, as suggested by the hon. member for Brandon, it would not have time to do anything else. This requires full-time operation by very large staffs of people to look after it, and to provide the house with up to the minute information on changes and developments in aircraft, ammunition, guns,
Supply-National Defence equipment and the like, would very soon weary the house and prevent it from doing anything else. We also assume that hon. members have available to them the ordinary information that appears in the press or in magazine articles.
Reference was made by the hon. member for Calgary East to the F-86E aircraft, in which he questioned the statements that had been made about the superiority of this aircraft. The fact is, as I understand it, the new F-86E aircraft have earned a combat ratio of nine to one over the MIG-15 in Korea. That is quoted in the white paper, from the actual words of the report of the Hon. Robert Lovett, former secretary of defence in the United States.
The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre again referred to our playing down the armoured corps. There is no intention of doing that and there is no indication of that being done. Everyone appreciates the great importance of armour and its proper place in any fighting team. What we have said is that it would not be in accordance with Canadian practice and would not meet the wishes of the Canadian people to have a Canadian armoured brigade which was not capable of operating independently. A brigade group which would be capable of operating independently would be a very large and much more costly team than what we have.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext: What does the minister mean by saying that an armoured brigade cannot operate independently? Under what circumstances would he expect it to operate independently? Armoured brigades normally co-operate with infantry formations. Could not Canadian armoured brigades co-operate with British divisions in this way?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext:
Yes; but in peacetime in Germany, in order to have it exist, it would be necessary to integrate it very closely indeed with British units, British formations, so that it would have the services of supply, R.C.E.M.E., signals, army medical corps, hospital, post office and all the other services that our brigade groups have in order to permit them to operate independently. If you added all this to an armoured brigade so as to make it what I understand an armoured brigade group to be it still could not operate independently; it would operate always in conjunction with one or two infantry divisions, whereas our brigade group is in effect a small division with armour, with artillery, with signals, with engineers, capable of operating independently, and until recently it actually has been so set up as part of the army reserves.
3982	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence Finally the hon. member for Calgary East referred again to some of the remarks that have been made about the equipment of the reserve forces. This has been gone over time and time again and I have no intention of going over the ground at length. But I must say this. We at national defence headquarters-and when I say "we" I mean the officers advising me, the chief of the general staff, the adjutant general, the quartermaster general-know of no shortage of equipment such as those referred to by the hon. member. They had not been called to my attention before except in the article in the Calgary Herald. What is extraordinary is that they had not been called to our attention in the meetings of the reserve association.
The meeting of the artillery reserve association took place in October after these changes had been promulgated. I have their resolutions here. Not one of them refers to any shortage of equipment for training. We met the officers of the association, and exchanged views in the freest possible way, as is the practice, and this was never raised. Then, later, the conference of defence associations met in a three-day session at Ottawa, and raised every conceivable question they could, bearing on the work and the good relations of the reserve forces. No question of this kind was raised by them.
What was done was that, in order to permit artillery regiments to make the best possible use of equipment that could be supplied to them for training purposes, the general officers commanding were given a pool of guns on the basis of entitlement of four 25-pounders per unit, where a regiment was located in one spot. That was done so as to reduce the amount of equipment on charge, to reduce maintenance costs and to reduce the need for storage space. There is no shortage of 25-pounders. We have been giving them away to our European allies and we still have ample left to meet all our needs until such time as they are replaced by 105's out of our own production.
With regard to tractors the entitlement was precisely the same, that is, four per regiment. Again there is no shortage. It is entirely up to the discretion of the general officer commanding. If one of the regiments has three instead of four, then no doubt it has been due to the exercise of discretion by the general officer commanding, or to the fact that one was being repaired, or for some other reason.
In respect of jeeps, we have decided to replace service jeeps for operational training with more modern types. That was done by putting in the hands of general officers commanding pools of jeeps to be used for this 

purpose. That was begun simultaneously with the beginning of their withdrawal, to renovate them and send them abroad. However, to replace jeeps at regimental headquarters used for administrative purposes, vehicles of commercial types have been issued. That issue is 80 per cent complete, and should be completed within the next month.
I hope I have answered all the questions, but if I have not perhaps we could deal with them when we are discussing the details.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext: What about anti-tank regiments?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext: I am sorry; I had forgotten to mention that. It is a difficult question; but the role of anti-tank regiments is a matter being considered by the British, the Americans and ourselves in close conjunction. It has not yet been decided, so far as Canada is concerned, whether this role will be carried out by armour or by artillery. However, it looks to me as if the old self-propelled antitank gun will be replaced right across the board by armour-that is, by tanks. As hon. members know, there has been very little difference between the two. The tanks we are getting have heavier and more powerful guns. However, so far as we can judge, the units will be the same, and will occupy the same roles, but will simply change their names.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext: Does the minister mean that likely they will be transformed from artillery units to armoured corps units?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext: That point is still receiving consideration. I said it was likely. However, I do not like to anticipate military decisions that have not yet been made, and the matter is still receiving consideration.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext: As reported at page 3822 of Hansard I asked a question regarding the plan being followed in the construction of permanent and non-permanent buildings. I should like to ask a further question before the conclusion of the general
Supply-National Defence discussion. My question arises from a statement made last night by the minister when he was discussing the present staff establishment of the deputy minister. The general explanation the minister gave for the fact that at the present time the staff of the deputy minister exceeds the total of the three staffs of the three deputy ministers for the navy, the army and the air force during the war years was that a number of functions formerly discharged by the strictly civil administration are now assumed by the deputy minister's office.
Perhaps I have not put it quite accurately; but the point I had in mind was that, as the minister said, while the three services were formerly responsible for the preparation of their own estimates, that is now done by the deputy minister's office. As I followed the minister giving the figures of the differences that would be accounted for by changes in function, I came to a total of approximately 50 which would be accounted for by increase in function within the office of the deputy minister, which would mean that at the present time, comparing the size of the staffs to the staff of the three deputies during the second world war, there would be 64 people in the office of the deputy minister now doing the same sort of jobs that were done during the war by 98, which was the maximum on the staffs of the three deputies. I know that a straight mathematical calculation does not always give rise to a valid comparison, but the discrepancy is still so large that I would ask the minister to give some further explanation.
If you take 64 on the staff of the deputy minister doing the same jobs that were previously done by 98 and then bear in mind the size of the forces today as being approximately 100,000, you get a ratio of about 1 to 1,500, whereas if you take 98 on the staffs of the three during wartime and divide them into the number in the services during the active stages of the war, being approximately 900,000, you get approximately 1 to 9,000. Therefore your ratio is 1 to 1,500 as against 1 to 9,000. It is a sufficiently impressive difference that I think we should ask the minister for some further explanation as to whether in fact there is not a tendency to increased staff which is not warranted by the size of the operations being undertaken.
Last night the minister, in starting that portion of his remarks dealing with the problem, gave the following explanation in partial justification for the tendency to increase staff. He said, as reported at page 3925 of Hansard:
Hon. members have referred a great deal to the Currie report, and some hon. members have heard
3984	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence that report discussed before the special committee on defence expenditures. They will find from the evidence that the statement I made in the house on January 13 was completely confirmed, that is, that a major factor in the lack of control which gave rise to my appointing Mr. Currie and the making of his report was the lack of sufficient staff to do the job. Actually we are understaffed today in the Department of National Defence.
That is the minister's statement, which must be read in the light of the fact that there is this disparity in the ratio of the deputy minister's staff to men on strength as between now and wartime of 1 to 1,500 as against 1 to 9,000. This also makes me ask the minister for a further explanation when I read that statement which I have just quoted in the light of what the minister was saying back in 1948 as to the basis on which Canada's defence forces were then being organized. In 1948, I might point out, we were appropriating approximately $250 million for defence purposes, which was a very large figure up to that time for peacetime establishments. The minister, in outlining Canada's defence objectives and programs and the reason why that amount was being asked for, made the following statements as reported at pages 5784 and 5785 of Hansard for June 24, 1948:
Against this background it is now possible to set down Canada's present defence aims and objectives. They are: ... (2) to provide the operational and administrative staffs, equipment, training personnel and reserve organization which would be capable of expansion as rapidly as necessary to meet any need.
Then at page 5785 he said:
Our plans are being made now for up to five and even ten years ahead, with changes provided for to meet expected developments.
Then a little later he said, "Our plans are flexible." Finally, at the bottom of the first column on that page there is the following: Secondly, the active army is to provide the administrative and training staff-the cadre of officers, N.C.O.'s and tradesmen-to train the reserve army and with it form the nucleus for as large a force as Canada may need.
With reference to the first quotation from 1948, namely to provide the operational and administrative staffs, equipment, training personnel and reserve organization which would be capable of expansion as rapidly as necessary to meet any need, I realize of course that this must be read and taken in the light of the fact that it was pre-Korea, and that the staff then actually in being had to deal with personnel numbering in the neighbourhood of perhaps 35,000. But it must obviously be-and I think this is surely a correct statement-in the contemplation of any minister or department of national defence and their planning staffs that their eventual job in the final analysis is to meet what may happen but which we hope will 

not happen, the eventuality of war. Therefore when the minister said "would be capable of expansion as rapidly as necessary to meet any need" I think we must take it that ultimate eventuality was in mind.
We are left confronted with the situation that two years prior to Korea the minister said that plans were being made then to provide the staff and administrative organization capable of expansion as rapidly as necessary to meet the need and form the nucleus for as large a force as Canada might need. One can understand that in 1950, on the outbreak of the Korean war, there would necessarily be a considerable period when expansion of the organization lagged behind the immediate requirements. That would be inevitable and necessary and not open to criticism; nevertheless the possibility of a shooting war must have been foreseen, although not in the exact form it has taken, and it seems to me that we require an explanation as to why in 1953, three years after Korea, the minister is still saying that "actually we are understaffed today in the Department of National Defence".
Two years before Korea, five years ago, we were told that Canada's defence program then provided for a staff capable of expansion as rapidly as necessary to meet any need. The need arose in 1950, two years after that statement; but now, three years after the eventuality which occurred in 1950, we are still told that we are understaffed.
I put. these considerations before the committee and the minister because, while I know we cannot be dogmatic in these matters and cannot be unfair, it does seem to me that the situation, with all the serious consequences of a breakdown as revealed in the Currie report-a breakdown which might not have exposed the department to criticism had it been confined to the first year following the outbreak in Korea-does raise very serious considerations when we find it still continuing three years after the outbreak in Korea, especially in the light of what the minister said two years before that outbreak.
It seems to me that it also requires quite a lot of reconciliation of the circumstance that we find at the present time in one part of defence headquarters, the staff of the deputy minister, numbers of staff giving us a ratio of 1 to 1,500 men in the forces against a ratio of only 1 to 9,000 during the period of active war. I would ask the minister to please enlarge on the difficulties and give us some explanation of why it is that he is compelled to say, three years after Korea, that they are still understaffed in the Department of National Defence.

I would be very glad to, Mr. Chairman. The reason is that the operations, measured in terms of construction and acquisition of equipment-that is, measured in terms of material or money-have been much larger since Korea than they were at any comparable period of the second world war. They consequently have required and should have required a larger staff. Unfortunately we have not had that larger staff and, as Mr. Currie said, there was a breakdown of the accounting, not in the department but in a single branch, the army works services. That was something we knew before. Mr. Currie did not tell us that because it had been reported on before and we were seeking to get staff to remedy the situation. We are still short of staff and having difficulty in getting it.
With regard to the size of the deputy minister's staff, ratios are very interesting indeed; but with an operation of the size and nature we have with the navy, army and air force totalling 104,000, located in six different countries, carrying on all the operations of training and fighting and doing those in peacetime, then I suggest that you have a situation which is far more complex in character, though not nearly as large in size, than anything that existed in the first or second world wars.
The office of the deputy minister of national defence today in its burdens, in its day to day grind, in the volume of work that he has to see to and also in the number of conferences with other countries and other departments at which he must be represented, I venture to say is at least as great as the sum of that of his three predecessors in the department. When we co-operate with the United States and Great Britain so closely it may take only one man to represent Canada for any one purpose, but it does take one. Because Canada has one-fifteenth of the effort of the United States, or whatever the fraction is, it does not mean that we can send one-fifteenth of a man to a conference. We still have to be represented by one man, and that is the reason ratios are not so relevant in this regard.
With regard to the build-up, we have always had these objectives. In 1948 the objective was to get staff to do the job. The staff was just good enough and just big enough to enable us to get into the Korean business without too great dislocation. What we are doing today is representative of about 25 per cent of the war effort. It is about 25 per cent, measured in terms of men, money and materials, of our wartime activity.
Having raised the Korean force we were immediately faced with the consequences of having done the job pretty quickly and then,

This includes, of course, the classified employees plus the casual and prevailing rate help.
In terms of numbers, the classified establishment of civilian staff presents some rather interesting increases. These estimates show a total of 25,090 civilian staff plus, according to the white paper, approximately 19,800 currently engaged as casuals and prevailing rate help. The total classified civilian staff for the current year represents an increase of about 22 per cent over the past year, an increase in numbers of about 4,460 people. I notice that as between the past fiscal year and the year prior to that there was an increase of 30 per cent, again an increase in the total number of civilian personnel of 4,835. The minister has given an explanation as to why the civilian personnel engaged in administration increased so sharply. It was mainly due to an increase in the inspection staff. However, in the total number of civilians employed in the Department of National Defence, we have some rather remarkable increases in what you might call the junior classifications.

I notice that in the matter of typists we have an increase as between last year and the current year of 518, the total being 1,861. This figure corresponds roughly, I believe, to about one civilian typist for every man we have engaging the enemy in Korea. Percentagewise the number of typists has increased 39 per cent compared with last year.
I might add, however, that there has been a decrease in one type of civilian help which, while I am glad to see it, may perhaps not be for the best in the light of the large increase in the number of typists. I refer to the number of civilian typewriter inspectors and repair men employed. In this category we have a 25 per cent decrease compared with last year. The number dropped from a total of 12 to a total of 9. In another classification we have stenographers. During the current year the total number of stenographers engaged by the department in the civilian establishment is 1,345, which is an increase of 253 compared to last year. Percentagewise it is an increase of 25 per cent in that particular class. In the classification of clerk we have an increase over last year of 931 the present total being 4,471. This represents a percentage increase of about 27 per cent in that category. According to the white paper the members ot the active force currently engaged in our commitments under NATO, for Korea and for the defence of Canada number about 43,200, whereas we have in the classification of administration just over 25,000 civilian employees, something like 6,000 service personnel engaged in commands and administration, and of course an additional 19,800 civilian employees in the category of casual and prevailing rate. This makes a total of 50,800 civilians or military personnel who may be said to be engaged in administration. This figure of 50,800 exceeds by a very substantial degree the total number of active service personnel, 43,200, who are actually engaged under NATO, for our Korean commitments or in the defence of Canada. Supply-National Defence employees, are going to be reflected in any comparable increase percentagewise this year in the number of men actually engaged in the active forces of our country?

Well, sir, the activities of the men engaged in Korea have, as the hon. member knows, no relationship to the number of stenographers, and vice versa. I do not need to press that point. The fact is that we have tried to get just as big a proportion of the job of national defence done by civilians as possible, for reasons which I have made clear on a number of occasions. Upon comparison I find that we have just about the same proportion of service to civilian personnel as they have in the United Kingdom and in the United States; that is about 1 to 2.5, one civilian to 2.5 service personnel. Since we believe the number of operational troops is comparable, that would seem to be, on any basis of comparison, a fair result.
With regard to the various categories which the hon. member mentioned, as he knows the establishments are set up only after an examination by the civil service commission. We have working in the commission a team consisting of service personnel, representatives of the deputy minister, of the treasury board and of the civil service commission itself. They look and see whether or not it is necessary to have an additional employee in any spot. Before an additional employee is appointed the establishment has to be created. I can assure the hon. member that there are far more refusals to create an establishment than there are approvals. This can be turned down at probably 15 to 20 stopping places before it gets approved. However, in the last result, if it does pass the civil service commission it then has to be approved by the treasury board, which has its own officers right in our department checking up to ensure the greatest possible efficiency. Therefore if a civilian establishment is created it is because a job needs to be done and it is usually created about six to nine months after it is first requested.
With regard to typewriter repairs, they are done to the greatest possible extent under contract. We hope to get out of the typewriter repair business ourselves as much as we can. These typewriter inspectors are able to service typewriter machines. We try to replace civilians by civilians in continuing non-combatant jobs, and we also try to replace service personnel by civilians in continuing non-combatant jobs. In the work of ordnance depots and other similar activities, we should like to see the depots run or managed by civilians with as few service personnel as possible in order to secure continuity and a professional attitude

While it is not public funds, the auditing and the administration of those stores is a matter for which staff officers have to take a certain amount of responsibility. It takes a great deal of their time which could normally be devoted to training, to organization, or, as we used to say, to getting on with the war.
It seems to me a very strong case could be made for the establishment under our military set-up here of an organization similar to the NAAFI in the United Kingdom. I have had a number of officers in the permanent camps complain to me that they had to spend so many hours per month auditing the books or answering complaints of soldiers' wives about goods they had bought in the grocery store. That is something which should be taken away from the military side and put on the civilian side, or put on some sort of permanent basis. The training officers, the responsible officers in these camps should not have to be bothered with the organization of these grocery stores and other stores that serve the civilian personnel. Can the minister say whether that is under consideration, or whether anything is likely to be done about it?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext: Yes, it is under consideration. We have a great number of establishments in the navy, army and air force. We try to keep them on about the same lines in so far as their functions are the same. At isolated centres they have to operate stores. These stores are usually operated by regimental institutes, or the like. We have given a great deal of consideration to the introduction into Canada of a system like NAAFI. We were going to call it CAAFI in Canada, but we have decided not to do it at once but to look further into the possibility of introducing this type of civilian organization to operate service stores and establishments. Of course this is all outside government moneys.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext: Yes, I realize that.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext:
And they are profitable
institutions. The question is how they are to be operated. Who is to operate them and who is to get the profit from them? And of
Supply-National Defence . course who is to control them? Well, the navy and the air force are quite content with their service set-up. The army would prefer to have something corresponding to NAAFI, and these differences relate quite a lot to the difference in function of the three services. The navy has ships which do not quite fit into the ordinary NAAFI pattern. The air force does things very well in its permanent stations. The army feels it would be desirable to have these stores operated by a civilian agency.
We have given a great deal of thought to that; we have had a great deal of experience on it in the post-war period in the three services in Germany, in France and in England, as well as in the Far East. I can say that the matter has been given very close consideration indeed. The great thing must be to secure effective control of an efficient operation. So far we believe that we have both the effective control and the .efficient operation; but it might be more effective and more efficient as regards the army at least if it were put more in civilian hands.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext:
My point in raising the question was the amount of time that has to be spent by the executive headquarters staff at a camp like Petawawa or Borden in looking after these stores. speechtext: I do not find in any item a total figure such as the one he mentioned. It would be necessary to go through these items and get the information he has requested.

Royal Canadian Navy-Active force and general.

speechtext: I see here five items for gardeners totalling about $50,000. Why does the navy have to spend that amount of money on gardeners? Are they attending marine gardens? It does seem unusual, particularly in the navy.

speechtext: Hon. members know that the navy derived some of its best support during the second world war from the wheat farmers of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba. Perhaps some of the so-called gardeners are there. This relates to the work of keeping in order the grounds at Esquimalt on the west coast-which are quite considerable, I might say, but still inadequate-as well as those at Halifax in the east, and at Dartmouth across the harbour. Then there are 22 naval reserve divisions, all of which have grounds to be kept in order. subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext: So far as I can see the other services do not have expenditures for gardeners. It is somewhat incongruous to find the navy, which is supposed to operate at sea, with this expenditure for gardeners.

speechtext: I find at page 304 of the details several items for gardeners in that part of the estimates concerning the army.

speechtext: In my day in the army the defaulters used to do that sort of work.
