subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext:
When I spoke the day before yesterday I referred to the conversion of the former destroyer Algonquin to an escort vessel, and pointed out that the work of changing her from her former role was carried out by Yarrows at Esquimalt. According to a statement made at one time by

the minister the Algonquin was to be the prototype of other vessels which were to play a similar role. Then the next vessel to be converted from a destroyer to that of an escort vessel, namely the Crescent, had her conversion carried out at the dockyard at Esquimalt.
It seems to me the experience gained at Yarrows in connection with the original conversion, and in drawing up the prototype plans, was lost when the second vessel was taken to H.M.C. dockyard at Esquimalt for conversion. Surely it would have been more profitable to have the same work carried out at the same shipyard, instead of going to a competitor in the form of a government-sponsored dockyard. If the information I have received is correct, the original contract for Crescent was given to Yarrows, but after the work had been started it was switched to the dockyard. Surely that type of operation not only discourages the civilian shipyards but also means delays in production. There must have been delays in the converting of the second vessel. Would the minister tell me why the switch was made from Yarrows to the dockyard?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, perhaps I might be permitted to deal with the hon. member's question. The conversion of the Algonquin, as he states, was done at Yarrows, and reconversion of the Crescent at the naval dockyard is following the same pattern. It is my understanding that when a lead yard -and we try to keep a number of them fully occupied-does a job such as was done on the Algonquin the plans and specifications and all the details of what has been done become the property of the navy and may be used in any other yard.
That is the first point. The second point is that the maritime commission keeps under surveillance all the different lead yards in Canada, and the disposition is to see that they are all occupied as far as is reasonably possible. With respect to reconversion of the Crescent, whatever yard might do the work would, as I have said, have the advantage of all the work that was done at Yarrows because all plans and specifications accrue to the crown. The disposition of these ships made by the maritime commission is such that they go to different yards at different times for different purposes in order that all lead yards may be reasonably utilized.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext:
I presume the minister
realizes that Yarrows shipyards are a private concern whereas the dockyard is government-owned and in this case is in direct competition in shipbuilding with the civilian shipyard located in the same city. I should

think that the original purpose of the dockyard was to repair government ships, and it is hardly its role to enter into the shipbuilding business and undertake work which is normally performed by private shipyards, I think the minister will agree with me that the job done by Yarrows on the Algonquin was excellent, and there would seem to be very little encouragement for the civilian shipyard on the west coast where there are not too many orders, I can assure you. Men have been laid off by Yarrows because of these switches of contracts, according to the information I have received from these yards.
I feel that very little encouragement is offered to the civilian shipyard to go into naval construction if, after having had all the difficulties of producing the prototype vessel, the next vessel, in connection with which they could have utilized the experience gained by their draftsmen and technicians in producing the first vessel, which would make it easier for the shipyard to produce the second, is taken away from them and given to a government dockyard. I hope the minister will bear in mind that it is most essential that we keep shipyards on the west coast alive, and I think some restraint must be exercised in giving orders to the government dockyard in preference to the private enterprise shipyards.
I do not know that I can say any more about it. I do feel that is a consideration which should be borne in mind. Does the Minister of Defence Production wish to say something?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext: My hon. friend suggests that the lead yard should do all the work in the type of vessel in which it leads. Of course that is not the idea of preparing Canada for war. We try to give several shipyards experience in the type. For instance, Vickers is the lead yard in the new type of escort destroyer and perhaps could turn them out like sausages, but instead of that we have several yards working on the escort destroyer, including two yards on the west coast. The purpose is to build up an industry that has the technique to meet a war situation. That explains the Algonquin and why the sister ship, the Crescent, was put in another yard. My hon. friend says we should always use private industry in preference to government industry.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext: I did not say that.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext:
I can assure him that we have civilians working in both, and they all have to be kept employed. As a matter of fact, about a third of our war contracts for ships are placed on the west coast, which is about
Supply-National Defence the proportion that should be placed there. 1 think the yards on the west coast engaged in purely naval work are employed to the full extent of any yards in the east. Of course some of the eastern yards supplement such construction by commercial work which they find through their own initiative, but I doubt very much if an analysis of purely naval work would show any lack of attention to the west coast.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext:
Of course I did not say that all the work should be given to civilian shipyards. The minister put words in my mouth which I never used, and the record will show that. All I am saying is that a fair share of the work should be given to the civilian shipyards, and I question very much whether there was any advantage in this particular case in placing the second vessel in the government dockyard rather than giving it to one of the civilian shipyards. There are two shipyards in Victoria, but instead of giving the second vessel to one or other of them it was given to the dockyard.
However, the explanation has been given and the contract has been let. We cannot take it back. I can only express my regret that some consideration was not given to the civilian shipyards, and I can only hope that in future the civilian shipyards, as opposed to the government dockyard, will be given their full share of shipbuilding construction. If we are in a hurry, and if we are anxious to get these vessels built by the target date, we Shall have to take full advantage of the experience that has been gained.
The second point I want to discuss is the question of the removal of the magazine from Colwood to Rocky Point. According to information I have, which information has been given in the house and in the press, the Colwood magazine is being removed to Rocky Point. I think Rocky Point is somewhere between 15 and 20 miles to the west of Esquimalt. Colwood magazine is located on the western side of Esquimalt harbour.
Can the minister say when Colwood magazine was completed and how much its construction cost? My recollection is that it was only built in recent years at very considerable expense. It is not a storage but an expenditure magazine. It is not for the purpose of storing reserves of ammunition but merely to have sufficient ammunition on hand to replenish the supplies carried on vessels which may be expended during training or operation. The main reserve magazine is at Kamloops, and in the past the reserves have been railed to the expenditure stores at Colwood.
According to our information the magazine is being moved to Rocky Point, which is an
3992	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence exposed promontory of pretty flat ground. As it is outside the inner defences of Esquimalt harbour, ships that come into Esquimalt harbour will be required to move around to Rocky Point where additional jetties will have to be built, and where there will be very limited if any opportunities for concealing ammunition stores. If this ammunition was going to be placed back in the hills farther inland and concealed I could understand the advantage of moving it from Colwood; but they are placing these buildings on an exposed and very conspicuous promontory of land.
The expenditure, we have been told, is to be somewhere between $5 and $6 million, which is a pretty considerable expenditure of money. I do not know whether that will cover all the construction work. I would like to know when the Colwood magazine was completed, and the real reasons which are behind the move of this magazine from Colwood to Rocky Point.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, may I make a few observations with regard to the hon. member's question regarding shipyards on the west coast. I am reasonably familiar with the situation, I think, and the principal shipyards are being constantly surveyed by the maritime commission and are all being kept busy. I happened to be in Vancouver last week when they took the hull of one of the new destroyer escorts from the Burrard shipyard at Vancouver to Yarrows at Esquimalt for completion there. I think careful investigation by the hon. member would show that all the principal yards are kept busy.
The reconstruction of the Algonquin was not reconstruction as a ship but rather reconversion in many respects including the electronic side. The naval dockyard has the capacity to do that type of work. The desire generally is to keep all shipyards reasonably busy for the reasons which the Minister of Defence Production has mentioned. I think that is being done on the west coast and probably on the east coast as well.
With regard to the Rocky Point magazine, my information is that there were three major reasons for the establishment of this magazine. It is a large project, admittedly, but it is located in a district where there is not now and where there is not likely to be any housing development or expansion of the rapidly growing city and its environs, and therefore there is a large safety belt around the magazine. That is important. Also a study of the terrain, according to the experts, has shown that it is suitable to the type of construction envisaged. Lastly, the magazine is close to Esquimalt, which facilitates transportation of ammunition from ships coming


in for overhaul or maintenance. They take all the ammunition off, I understand, when a ship goes into the yards for refit, and pick it up later. The new magazine will be a permanent installation of some magnitude to serve Esquimalt in the future.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext:
It is some considerable distance from Esquimalt, as I have already pointed out, and it will mean that the vessels which have been in to Esquimalt will have to go out again.
There is another point in connection with it, and that is that the area of Rocky Point has been served in the past by country roads which have not been constructed in any way to meet heavy traffic such as is bound to occur during the construction of this magazine and when the ammunition is being put into the stores. That is what is known as an unorganized area. There is no municipality there. The roads are country roads with country bridges, and there is a prosperous farming area lying between the city of Victoria and Rocky Point known as the Metchosin district. The residents in that area are not in a position to maintain their roads, bridges and so forth in order to carry the heavy traffic which is inevitable when the construction period starts.
I hope that in the $5 million to $6 million being set aside for the construction of the storehouse, the roads within the area, the jetties, the administrative buildings and so on, provision is also made to assist the district in maintaining the roads leading from Esquimalt or Victoria into that area even though the approaches are outside of the actual property which the department has bought; because I can assure you, Mr. Chairman, that it is quite beyond the capabilities of that rural district to develop roads in order to carry the heavy traffic and then to maintain them when all that heavy military traffic is being carried. Has a sum of money been included in the estimates in order to maintain the approaches to that magazine?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext: We have not arrived at the stage of allocating various amounts of money for specific purposes, but I can assure the hon. member that his representations in regard to that question will certainly receive attention.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext:
Thank you. That will be very much appreciated because I know it is a real need.
The only other question I have to ask under this item is in respect of the hours of work of certain classes of civilian employees in the dockyard and at Naden. Can the minister tell me whether the majority of the employees in the dockyard and the civilian employees at

Naden are on the 40-hour week, and whether the firemen employed in those establishments are also on the 40-hour week? I have had numerous letters sent to me complaining of the hours which the firemen are expected to work in the dockyard or at Naden, and that they exceed the 40-hour week which I believe is generally in vogue in so far as employees on the Pacific coast are concerned. I believe that it applies to the majority of other classes employed in the dockyard and at Naden, but can the minister tell me?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, as I think the hon. member knows, in establishments in which the Department of National Defence employs civilians, the kind of worker who works in a civilian occupation, the rates are fixed by the Department of Labour on the basis of rates and conditions of service prevailing in the community. Hence we have the description "prevailing rates employees". The Department of National Defence conforms to the general pattern of government policy as determined by the regulations, and the Department of Labour is asked to advise the Department of National Defence, and then the treasury board, whether the conditions of work including the hours of labour and rates of pay are correct. In that respect we follow whatever is the pattern of civilian employment in the community.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext: I realize that, but from the information I have received, and I might say petitions which I have received from the employees, they feel that they are not receiving the same privileges that are granted to civilian firemen in the area; and the prevailing hours of work are not applied to the firemen at Naden and the dockyard. The hours of work which they are asked to carry out are governed more by the hours of work carried out on the Atlantic coast, and they do not conform to the prevailing hours of work and rates of pay on the Pacific coast. I would ask the minister to look into that matter and see that the prevailing rates, as they exist on the Pacific coast, are applied to the firemen in the naval establishments on the west coast.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext: I would be very glad indeed to look into that further.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext:
I only have a couple of questions to ask, and before the minister arrived I was going to ask them of the associate minister. I am glad to see him getting into harness, and I want to congratulate him on the new position he occupies. I should like to bring to the attention of the associate minister, as well as the minister, the fact that we have been promised a naval barracks for some time. I see a large amount in the estimates for buildings, and 1 was wondering whether or not our naval barracks would be
Supply-National Dejence included for erection this season. I understand that a site has been selected by the minister himself. I should like him to say whether or not this deal has gone through, and whether the naval barracks will be erected this season.
At the same time I should like him to say whether or not we are to get the new armouries we are expecting. I am not pleading with the minister that he is spending too much money. I see there is a large amount in the estimates for this purpose, and I thought we might as well get what justly belongs to us on this occasion. Our naval men should have a good barracks for their training, and I am sure our soldiers deserve the very best building that can be provided. I thought this was the proper place to mention these things, and I would ask either the minister or his associate to reply.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext:
On the question of the location of the naval reserve division of Charlottetown, I can assure the hon. member that the premier of Prince Edward Island, the member before him and quite a few others have brought me around to the site. I have looked it over and I regard it as a very desirable site indeed. The only trouble is that it would cost much more than we have to put the site in condition so we could erect a barracks for the naval division there. The site is superb but the wharf around is broken away, and there has been a certain amount of silt-age in the passage in front of it. In addition to that most of the ground is fill, so that all the heavy construction would have to be put on piles. This would lead to considerable expense.
I recognize the need for a new site for our naval reserve division in Charlottetown. As I say, I have been there a good many times and I have seen it. I am familiar with every inch of the ground. But so far, having regard to other priorities, we have not seen fit to put an amount in the estimates to proceed with that work. I hope that some day we will have money for an expenditure of that kind. At the present time the naval reserve division is well housed in a building belonging to the provincial government. That government would like to get it back, but so far we have held on to it. I can assure the hon. member that the matter is receiving continuous consideration.
With regard to the army barracks, I may say that is one of the oldest in Canada. On the other hand it has been well maintained. It is well located, and we have a good many other places in Canada which need a barracks more than Charlottetown. Having served alongside the artillery that came from there in the first world war, and having met them

Supply-National Defence in the second, I can appreciate that this is a good place to put a new barracks some time.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext:
I should like to ask the minister a question that comes under the general discussion of the navy, but a similar question could be asked when we get to the section dealing with the army and another when we come to the air force. I can throw them all into one. At the end of the items dealing with the navy we come to a gross total, and then appears this entry:
Less the estimated amount to be paid from the special account and the estimated credits from transfers of equipment charged to mutual aid, $44,700,000.
That is on page 303. Similarly over on page 310, at the end of the section dealing with the army, there is the same entry only it amounts to $94,077,000. Likewise on page 316, at the end of the section dealing with the air force, there is the same entry, only in that instance the amount is $108,195,000. Those three entries, which in each case are subtracted from the gross total, add up to $246,972,000. By a little more simple arithmetic I find that the grand total of these major items we have been discussing is $1,960,159,633, which does not include those amounts that have been subtracted. In other words it appears to me that if it were not for these credits at these three points the actual total of this item would be not $1,960,159,633, but $2,207,131,633.
Will the minister comment on whether or not that is a correct analysis as to the total amount that is actually [DOT] being spent for the items included in this general item, and also would he explain what is involved and what the reason is for these subtractions by reference to a special account?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext: Well, Mr. Chairman, there has been a change proposed in these estimates with regard to the handling of the mutual aid account. This is described on page 30 of the white paper. I shall not weary hon. members by reading it, but I think the point made by the hon. member is covered by paragraph 167 on page 30, which reads as follows: Consequently, in the 1953-54 estimates, the detailed amounts in the service votes and the mutual aid vote together exceed the estimated appropriation requested by some $247 millions which is made up of $84 millions to be expended from the special accounts and the estimated transfers of equipment as mutual aid from stocks acquired by the services since April 1, 1950, amounting to $163 millions.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext:
I should like to ask the minister about an item that appears on page 301 of the estimates, the 11th line from the bottom of the page, "Professional and special services, corps of commissionaires". Mr. Chairman, I think the time has arrived when that organization should be brought under

some department of government. Members of the corps of commissionaires work for all departments of government. In addition they are employed in many cities around theatres, as doormen around hospitals and so on.
The corps of commissionaires are a group of old soldiers, the older fellows who have reached the days when they are no longer productive in industry; and they are taken then, in most of the provinces, by a private employment agency. Some smart fellow organizes that corps on a provincial scale, and he farms out their labour to any organization that desires watchmen. I notice that the Department of National Defence has an item of over $1 million in the naval section. They are employed around the airports and around public buildings under all departments of government.
I think the method employed of having these men work for private employment agencies who farm them out and make money off their labour should come to an end. I think the corps is sufficiently large at the present time that its members should be brought under some department of government, preferably the Department of Labour, so their duties could be made more uniform, their wages fixed at a more reasonable rate, and some uniformity brought into the question of remuneration as far as that corps is concerned. The organization at the present time leaves much to be desired, and it is badly confused because its members are working for different rates of wages in different provinces, and are working in the same provinces and in the same communities for different organizations.
I am not making any criticism of the item that appears here in the estimates. I am merely raising that general question for the benefit of the members of the cabinet. In my opinion the time has come when these people should be brought under some department of government and when some regulation should be brought about with regard to their employment and remuneration; and I say the proper department to handle that corps of commissionaires is the Department of Labour.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I shall be brief.
I wanted to comment on an article dealing with comments made by Vice-Admiral Mainguy and appearing in the Gazette of December 18. The reason I am using this article is that it would appear that not only is the naval program long delayed but, as to one item, it has cost about three times

what it was estimated to cost. The article reads in part:
Reviewing the navy's needs and plans for 1952, the admiral said:
And I quote paragraph 3.
3. Shipbuilding programs started in previous years will bring fruit, with four more of the new antisub escort vessels being launched-

-and the coastal minesweeper program of 14 vessels being completed.

In the white paper this sentence appears:
The northern patrol vessel, H.M.C.S. Labrador, originally scheduled for 1952, will be completed before the end of 1953.
The minesweepers were estimated to cost $950,000 each, 1 understand, and they have actually cost somewhere about $3 million. Is that correct or is it not?

speechtext: I wonder whether this is the time, while we are discussing naval estimates, when the Minister of National Defence would like to make a comment on the possibility that he might forward his training program in the navy by some kind of co-ordination between the naval program and the coastguard service which has been mooted many times in Canada as a desirable feature on both the Atlantic and the Pacific coasts. It has always occurred to me, particularly with vessels of the smaller type that we are speaking of, such as minesweepers, that perhaps the finest training we could give our younger sailors in naval tactics might be in co-ordinating the services of the navy and those of the coastguard. I should be grateful for a comment from the Minister of National Defence in regard to that suggestion, which I am sure has been made to him before.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS

Generally speaking I think it has been found in all navies that it is a good thing to have the young naval personnel receive their first training at sea in a naval vessel; and for that purpose we have training ships. Quite a large number of those in commission for the Royal Canadian Navy are specially earmarked as training ships. After that training period it might be desirable to work them in on other types of training including coastguard or the like if that exists; but that would have to be worked out.
With regard to the provision of coastguard service-and that is the question the hon. member really raises-that is a matter which concerns much more the Department of Transport, the Department of Justice through the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and other departments of government. At the present time the job of search and rescue, which is an important operation, is co-ordinated in Canada through the R.C.A.F., and it has the closest possible tie-in with the Royal Canadian Navy, the merchant marine and civilian enterprises of all kinds. So far, my colleagues who have been concerned with that aspect of the problem felt that the co-ordination of search and rescue under ICAO should be left with the Royal Canadian Air Force, and the other questions should be dealt with as they arise.

You have also to take into account the fact that if a service person is posted for more than a year to a post in Canada or abroad he is entitled to have his wife and family and furniture moved at the government's expense. Consequently we reduce to the minimum possible the amount of posting but in a time of active service, where we have ships on each coast doing various duties, where we want to avoid inflicting on any serviceman more than the minimum term of duty abroad and where

also we have to fit in his service abroad with his posting to take courses for promotion, the transportation expenses are apt to be high.
I am afraid that is an inevitable result of the geography of our country. I have yet to hear of a service person who has received what he regards as a fair recompense for his travel. That is regrettable, but it indicates that we are tough about it. speechtext: I realize that I cannot fairly expect the minister to give a detailed answer to what I asked, but what he has said has certainly interested me and makes me feel that I want to know a great deal more about this. subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext: After all that difference is not too important.

But I was

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext: Far more than that.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext: I want to know a little more about that, and perhaps the minister would give me a statement in some detail when the committee discusses this next. speechtext:

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS

speechtext: Perhaps they can be divided into classes and perhaps the minister can give us illustrations so we might understand better what is meant by the very imposing phrase "1,048 major projects". subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext: Well, Mr. Chairman, I was not too far out in my recollection of the figures. We prepared 39 standard designs for permanent construction for the three services. We have 28 designs for emergency buildings, and so far we have used 10 of those, all at Wainwright. It is quite easy to put on the record the places, the details of the type of construction and so on in each case, but my information is that this has been gone into before the committee on defence expenditure.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext:
We are not
allowed to talk about that.

speechtext: I am told that not only were you allowed to talk about it, but that you insisted on talking about it, and it was gone into at great length. However, if there is any item of information which the hon. member would like, we will certainly have it available for him.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I want to ask the minister about what appears to me to be the penultimate item under departmental administration and navy, "additional positions to be established". speechtext: The positions relate to inland stores depot, Montreal, for handling, packing, maintenance and inventory of the main R.C.N. stores depot, 425; maintenance of ships in inactive reserve at Sydney, Nova Scotia, including security and fire protection and servicing of dehumidifying plant, 80; at naval stores headquarters, Ottawa, an increase in office workers to provide necessary assistance for the administration of the expanding navy, 125; on the east coast in the dockyard, stores, depots, armament depots and magazines to meet the increased requirements of the fleet and to provide for the installation and maintenance of new equipment from current production, 460; on the west coast in the dockyard, stores, depots, armament depots and magazines to meet the increased requirements of the fleet and to provide for the installation and maintenance of new equipment from current production, 410.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext: Well, that is for the navy. I just added this up and there seems to be some discrepancy in the salaries. speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext:
While the minister is looking up the answer to this question, perhaps I might ask hon. members if I may have their co-operation. Two years ago we studied these details at the end of the book line by line. Last year it was suggested that we proceed heading by heading. Yesterday I asked hon. members if that procedure would be agreeable this year. I asked for comments upon that, and there were none. Hon. members agreed. We have discussed the first heading, which was departmental administration, including inspection service. Then I asked, shall we pass on to navy? If we carry on with questions under the details for half an hour and then have a wide-open question, and then return to restrictive questions, we shall never finish. subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext: In answer to the hon. member for York West, I might say that the difference is due largely to the proportion of technical staff on the side that he mentioned.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext:
A question has come up in the study of the white paper and the estimates, and it is this. Is our navy of such a nature that it requires far more administration than either of the other two services, the; army or the air force, both from the point qf jview of service personnel and civilian employees? In checking the figures presented by the minister, I find that in dealing with personnel of the active forces only, out of a total active force of 15,400 in the navy, 1,400 are listed under command and administration. Qf course there are additional numbers of men in training staffs and trainees, but I have not included them under administration.. On,,this basis of 1,400 in administration within the service, one . out of every eleven men in the navy is, engaged in command or administration.	.	. *	,*	, , ,,
In so far as the army is concerned, referring again to the figures on manpower presented in the white paper, one in every seventeen men is engaged , in administration. In the aiE force, only one in twenty-twp men is engaged in administration. In other words the air force requires half as much administration in terms of personnel. as the, navy.
Turning now to the classified establishments for civilian employees, I find that there is one civilian employed by the navy for every 2-3 members in the active forces; in the army there is only one civilian for every 5 -1 members, and the air force is almost three times as good as the navy and 50 per cent better than the army because they have only one civilian employed for every 7 * 4 members of the active air force. Can the minister explain the reasons for the very wide variation in the percentage of the total personnel, service and civilian, required for the handling of the administration in the three services?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext:
I am not ready to admit the computations the hon. member has made, but quite apart from that the navy have traditionally employed a very high percentage of civilian employees in their dockyards and similar activities. This is true of the Royal
Navy, the United States Navy and the Royal Canadian Navy. A very high degree of skill is required there, and that skill is usually related to some previous service in the navy, then service ashore in a civilian occupation of that kind. The navy very largely has these dockyard employees do the job of dealing with their ships, armaments, electronics and so on.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext: The minister referred to the prevailing rate employees and dockyard workers for the navy. subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext: The navy has a very high proportion of people who ip ordinary, industry would be prevailing rate employees, but who in the dockyards are leading hands and the like, timekeepers and so on, who are classified * civil servants.

speechtext: One of the larger items under navy is that for ammunition and bombs, which is $28,461,000 this year, and was $7,402,000 last year.
